channel.description: Debezium is an open source distributed platform for change data capture. Start it up, point it at your databases, and your apps can start responding to all of the inserts, updates, and deletes that other apps commit to your databases. Debezium is durable and fast, so your apps can respond quickly and never miss an event, even when things go wrong.

item.title: Debezium 3.6.4.Final Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
We’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.6.4.Final, the latest maintenance release of the 3.6 series, focused on stability and reliability.

This release is led by a round of fixes for the Oracle connector, resolving several cases where change events could be missed, most notably on Oracle RAC. Oracle deployments that capture many tables also benefit from a faster LogMiner query. Beyond Oracle, the release brings security updates through newer MySQL and MongoDB drivers, including a MySQL driver that addresses a published CVE.

Read on for the full details!

We’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.6.4.Final, the latest maintenance release of the 3.6 series, focused on stability and reliability.

This release is led by a round of fixes for the Oracle connector, resolving several cases where change events could be missed, most notably on Oracle RAC. Oracle deployments that capture many tables also benefit from a faster LogMiner query. Beyond Oracle, the release brings security updates through newer MySQL and MongoDB drivers, including a MySQL driver that addresses a published CVE.

Read on for the full details!

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium for MongoDB

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for MongoDB

MongoDB driver upgraded to 5.14

The MongoDB connector now ships with version 5.14.0 of the MongoDB Java driver, up from 5.9.2. The upgrade keeps the connector current with the driver’s latest fixes and requires no configuration changes. (dbz#3022)

Debezium for MySQL

MySQL Connector/J upgraded to 26.10.0

The MySQL driver that ships with the MySQL connector and the JDBC sink has been upgraded from 9.1.0 to 26.10.0. The previous version was affected by CVE-2025-30706, and the newest 9.x driver carries several more recent CVEs, so the upgrade moves directly to the 26.x line.

Most deployments need no changes, but there are two things worth knowing. Starting with 26.7.0, the driver’s release notes list MySQL Server 8.4 and later as supported. MySQL 8.0 is no longer in that documented range, although the driver does not reject it and the connector’s tests continue to pass against it.

The driver also now requires SSL keystores to be local files. The connector’s own SSL settings already work this way, so this only matters if you pass custom driver.* properties that point at a remote keystore URL. (dbz#3015)

Debezium for Oracle

Faster LogMiner query when capturing many tables

The query that the Oracle connector uses to read changes from LogMiner now handles schema and table lookups more efficiently, which reduces CPU overhead on the database and streams results faster. The benefit grows with the number of captured tables, so connectors with only a handful of tables will see little difference, while those capturing hundreds of tables gain the most.

The improvement applies when log.mining.query.filter.mode is set to in. The same rows are matched as before, and no configuration changes are required. (dbz#2991)

Other fixes

  • Schema history is restricted by snapshot.include.collection.list (dbz#1443)

  • Concatenated XML in a single Kafka message (dbz#2159)

  • SignalProcessor.executeWithSemaphore ignores the tryAcquire result and runs the critical section unguarded on timeout (dbz#2458)

  • JdbcSchemaHistory never commits open transactions on read paths (dbz#2579)

  • LogFileCollector exception is misleading when the Oracle archiver is slow to archive (dbz#2601)

  • TIME column with value 00:00:00 is emitted as null during the initial snapshot, but correctly as 0 during streaming (dbz#2631)

  • Allow including INTERNAL events for rollbacks to savepoint when lob.enabled=false (dbz#2666)

  • Physical standby always uses CURRENT_SCN for the upper boundary (dbz#2668)

  • SQL Server arithmetic overflow error on tables with more than 2.14 billion rows during a parallel chunked snapshot due to a hardcoded COUNT(1) (dbz#2670)

  • ExtendedStringParser assigns schema and table names in reverse order (dbz#2671)

  • SelectLobParser.reset() does not reset the inherited parser state (dbz#2672)

  • Update Hibernate to 7.4.10.Final (dbz#2681)

  • CloudEventsConverter may fail to initialize (dbz#2697)

  • PartitionRouting fails with NullPointerException when a nested field path traverses a null struct, such as before.name on INSERT events (dbz#2698)

  • Regression with relaxed quote DML parsing (dbz#2700)

  • ORA-02003: invalid USERENV parameter on Oracle 12 (dbz#2704)

  • SQL Server retriable task startup failure does not clean up allocated resources (dbz#2714)

  • Oracle XStream task fails after a restart (dbz#2782)

  • LogMiner on RAC silently skips change events at a capped log boundary SCN when another redo thread has an event at the same SCN (dbz#2862)

  • connection.pool.timeout is interpreted as milliseconds instead of seconds (dbz#2950)

  • LogMiner on RAC silently skips changes in a CLOSED redo thread when CappedLogFileSessionSelector truncates that thread’s logs (dbz#2957)

  • Heartbeat JDBC connection loses its PDB container after a reconnect because alter session set container is not replayed (dbz#2972)

  • Reread buffered LogMiner transactions so late LOB/XML rows are not lost (dbz#3039)

  • MySQL DDL parsing fixes (dbz#2673)

  • Oracle DDL parsing fixes (dbz#2656, dbz#2720)

In total, 35 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.6.4.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Akshat Sapra, Alvar Viana, Ayodya Enhanayoan, battmush, Bhuvan Somisetty, Chase Tingley, Chris Cranford, Divyanshu Kumar, Gaétan Collaud, Garib Karimli, Giovanni Panice, Gor Grigoryan, Jiri Pechanec, Minjae Lee, Robert Roldan, Sergei Nikolaev, Timur Rakhmatullin, Vojtech Juranek, Will Baker, and Zdravko Donev!

item.title: Debezium 3.7.1.Final Released
item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
We’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.7.1.Final, the first maintenance release of the 3.7 series, focused on stability and reliability.

This release resolves a number of cases where change events could be skipped or duplicated after a connector restart, and it restores pieces of the Debezium Server distribution that went missing in 3.7.0.Final. It also brings updated database drivers that address several recently published CVEs. If you use the Oracle connector, be sure to review the breaking changes before upgrading.

Read on for the full details!
item.content:encoded:
We’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.7.1.Final, the first maintenance release of the 3.7 series, focused on stability and reliability.

This release resolves a number of cases where change events could be skipped or duplicated after a connector restart, and it restores pieces of the Debezium Server distribution that went missing in 3.7.0.Final. It also brings updated database drivers that address several recently published CVEs. If you use the Oracle connector, be sure to review the breaking changes before upgrading.

Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.7.1.Final

Debezium for Oracle

Snapshot locks are held for the whole snapshot

The Oracle connector now holds its table locks until the snapshot has finished reading the data, rather than releasing them once the table schemas were captured. This protects an initial snapshot from most schema changes made while it runs, which is the usual cause of an ORA-01466 failure that forces the snapshot to start over.

The snapshot.database.errors.max.retries property has been removed, because retrying could never succeed. The connector reads every table at the position it recorded when the snapshot began, and Oracle rejects that query for as long as the table’s definition is newer than that position. Each retry therefore failed in exactly the same way.

With the default snapshot.locking.mode of shared, other sessions can still read and write the captured tables during the snapshot, so most deployments will not notice a difference. Schema changes that need exclusive access to a table now wait until the snapshot completes. Some non-blocking schema changes, such as ALTER TABLE …​ ADD COLUMN on Oracle 23.3 and later, are still allowed by this lock and can still interrupt a snapshot.

For environments where that is a concern, a new extended locking mode prevents all schema changes on the captured tables. The trade-off is that writes to those tables are also blocked until the snapshot completes, so it is best suited to snapshots taken in a maintenance window. The connector waits up to snapshot.lock.timeout.ms for each table lock, and fails the snapshot if a lock cannot be obtained in that time.

snapshot.locking.mode=extended snapshot.lock.timeout.ms=10000

When upgrading, remove snapshot.database.errors.max.retries from your connector configuration if you had set it. If you run schema changes against captured tables on a schedule, plan them outside of the initial snapshot. You can also set snapshot.mode to no_data and load the existing data with an incremental snapshot, which does not rely on a single point-in-time read. (dbz#2787)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for MongoDB

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium Server

Debezium Core

MariaDB Connector/J upgraded to 3.5.11

The MariaDB driver that ships with the MariaDB connector and the JDBC sink has been upgraded to 3.5.11. This picks up the fixes for CVE-2026-119210, CVE-2026-119276, CVE-2026-119280, and CVE-2026-119281, which were published at the end of October.

The new driver version also fixes a defect where the database password could be exposed through the connection URL reported by the driver. No configuration changes are required. (dbz#2998)

Debezium for MongoDB

MongoDB driver upgraded to 5.14

The MongoDB connector now ships with version 5.14.0 of the MongoDB Java driver, up from 5.9.2. The upgrade keeps the connector current with the driver’s latest fixes and requires no configuration changes. (dbz#3022)

Debezium for MySQL

MySQL Connector/J upgraded to 26.10.0

The MySQL driver that ships with the MySQL connector and the JDBC sink has been upgraded from 9.1.0 to 26.10.0. The previous version was affected by CVE-2025-30706, and the newest 9.x driver carries several more recent CVEs, so the upgrade moves directly to the 26.x line.

Most deployments need no changes, but there are two things worth knowing. Starting with 26.7.0, the driver’s release notes list MySQL Server 8.4 and later as supported. MySQL 8.0 is no longer in that documented range, although the driver does not reject it and the connector’s tests continue to pass against it.

The driver also now requires SSL keystores to be local files. The connector’s own SSL settings already work this way, so this only matters if you pass custom driver.* properties that point at a remote keystore URL. (dbz#3015)

Debezium for Oracle

Column reselection uses the physical standby

When the Oracle connector streams from a physical standby, the ReselectColumnsPostProcessor now runs its queries against the standby as well. Previously those queries always went to the primary database, even though the standby was already handling everything else for streaming.

This keeps the extra read load of reselecting column values off the primary, which is often the reason for capturing from a standby in the first place. The behavior applies automatically when capture.mode is set to physical_standby, and other capture modes continue to use the primary connection. (dbz#2444)

Debezium Server

Apache Pulsar client upgraded to 4.2.5

Debezium Server now packages version 4.2.5 of the Apache Pulsar client, up from 4.2.1. The older client bundled Bouncy Castle 1.84 libraries that security scanners flagged for a number of CVEs, including certificate validation issues. The new client bundles Bouncy Castle 1.86, which resolves those findings for the Pulsar libraries.

The Pulsar sink’s configuration and runtime behavior are unchanged. (dbz#2799)

Other fixes

  • Cannot replicate GTID transaction (dbz#694)

  • TIME types cannot be read on AWS Aurora when snapshot.fetch.size is set (dbz#1015)

  • State leaks from an aborted incremental snapshot to the next (dbz#1563)

  • Concatenated XML in a single Kafka message (dbz#2159)

  • Arrays of TIME(p) lose fractional seconds for p > 3 and throw DateTimeException when the JVM user.timezone is not UTC (dbz#2559)

  • Snapshot changes pre-1582 and BC values for DATE and for arrays of temporal types (dbz#2664)

  • Allow including INTERNAL events for rollbacks to savepoint when lob.enabled=false (dbz#2666)

  • Snapshot throughput regression on timestamp and timestamptz columns caused by reading them as text (dbz#2686)

  • Ensure connector cleanup runs when the coordinator shutdown fails (dbz#2709)

  • SQL Server retriable task startup failure does not clean up allocated resources (dbz#2714)

  • Infinity dates emit inconsistent values across snapshot, pgoutput, and decoderbufs (dbz#2721)

  • NullPointerException when calling the signal API (dbz#2732)

  • Rows are skipped after a restart when XA transactions are used (dbz#2738)

  • SMTs in the Debezium Server 3.7.0.Final image fail with NoClassDefFoundError: io/debezium/transforms/SmtManager (dbz#2740)

  • Outbox Event Router fails the task when table.expand.json.payload expansion fails instead of emitting the record unchanged (dbz#2743)

  • Outbox Event Router drops W3C baggage from the propagated tracing context (dbz#2753)

  • LTREE arrays containing NULL elements lose the entire value (dbz#2770)

  • Oracle XStream task fails after a restart (dbz#2782)

  • Pub/Sub message attributes include JSON quotes when debezium.format.header.schemas.enable=false (dbz#2783)

  • Embedded engine with JdbcOffsetBackingStore fails with ClassCastException in TransactionContext.load when provide.transaction.metadata=true (dbz#2786)

  • primary.key.fields does not work for record_header primary keys (dbz#2795)

  • Table cannot be resolved for an object ID on physical standbys when the dictionary file is out of sync (dbz#2798)

  • capture.instance include/exclude filter is applied after the start_lsn de-duplication, silently dropping a table with two capture instances that share a start_lsn (dbz#2800)

  • Debezium Server 3.7 silently ignores a connector.class that is not part of the distribution build, so external connectors in lib/ or EXTRA_CONNECTOR no longer start (dbz#2801)

  • datetime2 values are shifted forward during the spring-forward daylight saving time transition (dbz#2805)

  • Stopping and resuming an incremental snapshot does not work on Debezium Platform (dbz#2824)

  • Native image build fails because HttpNotificationChannel is not registered for reflection (dbz#2840)

  • JsonTableChangeSerializer does not persist table-level comments (dbz#2848)

  • Connector cannot resume from an offset without a GTID set when the server uses GTIDs (dbz#2852)

  • LogMiner on RAC silently skips change events at a capped log boundary SCN when another redo thread has an event at the same SCN (dbz#2862)

  • Schema history recovery skips every non-snapshot change when the stored offset has a NULL change_lsn (dbz#2867)

  • Incremental snapshot emits duplicate rows or drops the last row for datetime primary keys (dbz#2871)

  • Changes are lost on restart when lsn_events_processed is 1, or when the offset is stored at a transactional logical message (dbz#2889)

  • With decoderbufs, a BEGIN sharing the stored LSN uses up an lsn_events_processed skip and re-emits a processed row (dbz#2894)

  • SwapGeometryCoordinates SMT throws NullPointerException on MAP fields with null values (dbz#2896)

  • With the OpenLogReplicator adapter, all rows in a transaction get the same source.scn (dbz#2912)

  • ClassCastException in keyAsStruct for primitive record keys with primary.key.mode=record_key (dbz#2917)

  • Connector opens an extra idle JDBC connection per task for the bean registry even when no post-processor is configured (dbz#2924)

  • Nine-digit INTERVAL fractional seconds are incorrectly scaled in numeric mode (dbz#2945)

  • connection.pool.timeout is interpreted as milliseconds instead of seconds (dbz#2950)

  • Heartbeat JDBC connection loses its PDB container after a reconnect because alter session set container is not replayed (dbz#2972)

  • unavailable.value.placeholder should not replace NULL in the after image (__$operation = 4) of max-type columns (dbz#2974)

  • Schema build at connector start is quadratic with many tables because FieldNameSelector caches by Column (dbz#2982)

  • Connection string masking leaves percent-encoded credentials unmasked in logs (dbz#2983)

  • Debezium Server 3.7 keeps running after the engine has failed instead of exiting (dbz#3010)

  • GeometryFormatTransformer fixes (dbz#2706, dbz#2904)

  • TimezoneConverter fixes (dbz#2667, dbz#2723)

  • unavailable.value.placeholder with an invalid hex: value is not rejected by validation and fails or produces wrong bytes at runtime (dbz#2868, dbz#2990)

  • Oracle transaction cache performance improvements (dbz#2777, dbz#2780)

  • Apicurio converter and serde missing from the Debezium Server distributions (dbz#2791, dbz#2978)

  • Cassandra 5 CDC fixes (dbz#2540, dbz#2736, dbz#2792)

  • MariaDB DDL parsing fixes (dbz#2891)

  • MySQL DDL parsing fixes (dbz#373, dbz#2755)

  • Oracle DDL parsing fixes (dbz#2853)

In total, 87 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.7.1.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Alex Limontov, Alvar Viana, Anton Rino Bosco, Ayodya Enhanayoan, battmush, Bhuvan Somisetty, Bitthal Ladiwal, Björn Ångbäck, Chris Cranford, Daniil Zabludovsky, Danny Mican, Dilraj Vyas, Divyanshu Kumar, Dongmin Kim, Evan Volgas, Gennadi Litke, Giovanni Panice, Jaeyeon Park, Jan Mohr, Jiri Pechanec, João Almeida, Lingyang Ma, Maarten Vercruysse, Marcel Bruhn, Marcin Michalski, Mario Fiore Vitale, Matt Hejnas, Matthias Crauwels, Minjae Lee, Mohamed Elkholy, Nikita Kokitkar, Niteesh Kumar Pandey, Robert Roldan, Sangeet Mishra, Sergei Nikolaev, Thiago Garcia, Tommy Karlsson, Virag Tripathi, Will Baker, Yashi Srivastava, and Zdravko Donev!

item.dc:creator: Chris Cranford
item.description:
As the leaves fall and November gets underway, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.8.0.Alpha1, the first preview release of the 3.8 series.

This release introduces a new Elasticsearch sink connector. It also brings snapshot progress monitoring to Debezium Platform, a new default mode for the JDBC sink, and improvements across many connectors. There are also many bug fixes and a few breaking changes to review before upgrading.

Read on for the full details!
item.content:encoded:
As the leaves fall and November gets underway, we’re pleased to announce Debezium 3.8.0.Alpha1, the first preview release of the 3.8 series.

This release introduces a new Elasticsearch sink connector. It also brings snapshot progress monitoring to Debezium Platform, a new default mode for the JDBC sink, and improvements across many connectors. There are also many bug fixes and a few breaking changes to review before upgrading.

Read on for the full details!

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there can be breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.8.0.Alpha1

Debezium for MySQL

REAL columns are now emitted as FLOAT64

MySQL and MariaDB treat REAL as a synonym for DOUBLE unless the REAL_AS_FLOAT SQL mode is enabled. Debezium already emitted these columns as FLOAT64 during snapshots, but when a table’s DDL was captured while streaming, the column was emitted as FLOAT32, silently truncating values to about seven significant digits.

The connectors now map REAL to FLOAT64 in all cases, so the schema is stable across snapshot and streaming, and no precision is lost. Default values for REAL columns are emitted as doubles accordingly.

If your consumers or Schema Registry subjects expect a float schema for these columns, they will now see double, so check your compatibility settings before upgrading. Tables captured before this change keep their recorded schema until the table model is rebuilt by a new snapshot or a later DDL statement on that table. If you previously used the JdbcSinkDataTypesConverter with treat.real.as.double as a workaround, it is no longer needed. (dbz#2217)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

NULL elements are preserved in ENUM arrays

A PostgreSQL ENUM array containing a NULL element, such as ARRAY['plain', NULL], previously failed schema validation. The entire array was then emitted as null, and if the column was declared NOT NULL, the connector stopped.

The element schema for ENUM arrays is now optional, matching how all other array types are handled, so values like ["plain", null] are preserved.

Because the array element schema changes from required to optional, consumers using Avro and Schema Registry will see a new schema version for affected columns. (dbz#2771)

VARBIT(1) columns are now emitted as bits

PostgreSQL accepts an empty bit string (B'') as a valid, non-null value in a VARBIT(1) column. Debezium mapped these columns to a boolean, so an empty value was emitted as null, and a NOT NULL column caused capture to stop.

VARBIT columns of any length are now consistently mapped to the io.debezium.data.Bits semantic type, a BYTES schema. This keeps B'', B'0', B'1', and SQL NULL distinct from one another. Fixed-length BIT(1) columns are not affected and are still emitted as booleans.

If you capture VARBIT(1) or BIT VARYING(1) columns, the field schema changes from BOOLEAN to BYTES, so update any consumers or sink mappings that rely on a boolean value. (dbz#2772)

Debezium Server

Kafka sink delivery timeout now defers to the producer

The Kafka sink had two settings that controlled how long to wait for record delivery: the producer’s own delivery.timeout.ms and the sink’s wait.message.delivery.timeout.ms. Depending on how the two were set, the sink could fail a batch while the producer was still retrying, or the sink setting would never take effect at all.

The default for wait.message.delivery.timeout.ms is now 0, which means the sink waits for the producer to finish and relies solely on the producer’s delivery.timeout.ms.

If you relied on the previous 30 second default, configure the timeout through debezium.sink.kafka.producer.delivery.timeout.ms instead, or set wait.message.delivery.timeout.ms explicitly to restore the old behavior. (dbz#2597)

Zerobus sink event filter removed

The Databricks Zerobus sink introduced in 3.7 shipped with its own event filter, configured through the debezium.sink.zerobus.filter.* properties. Debezium’s standard mechanisms already cover the same cases, so the sink-specific filter has been removed.

If you configured debezium.sink.zerobus.filter.* properties, migrate them to the standard equivalents:

  • To skip operations, use skipped.operations, and use snapshot.mode=no_data to skip snapshot read events.

  • To filter by topic or header, use the Filter transformation with the TopicNameMatches or HasHeaderKey predicates.

  • To filter by value, use the Filter transformation with the new FieldValueMatches predicate.

Note that HasHeaderKey only checks whether a header is present, so there is currently no direct replacement for matching on a header value. (dbz#2915)

New Features and Improvements

The following covers all new features and improvements, grouped by connector component area.

Debezium Core

Debezium for MongoDB

Debezium for MySQL

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium for SQL Server

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Elasticsearch sink

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Debezium Platform

Debezium Server

Debezium for Spanner

Debezium for YashanDB

Container Images

Debezium Examples

Debezium Core

Claim-check storage for oversized events

A change event can exceed the Kafka producer or broker message size limit when columns hold very large values. Until now, the options were to raise transport limits, truncate the large values with the EnforceRecordSize transformation, or exclude the columns entirely and lose their data.

The EnforceRecordSize transformation now offers an opt-in claim_check strategy that works with any connector. When an event exceeds max.bytes, the complete original record is written to external storage, and the configured columns in the emitted event are replaced with a small marker that points to the stored object. The marker is only emitted after the write succeeds, so a failed write never results in a reference to data that wasn’t stored.

Storage is pluggable, and Debezium ships with an Amazon S3 implementation. The following example stores oversized records from the inventory.customers table in S3:

transforms=EnforceRecordSize transforms.EnforceRecordSize.type=io.debezium.transforms.EnforceRecordSize transforms.EnforceRecordSize.max.bytes=1048576 transforms.EnforceRecordSize.strategy=claim_check transforms.EnforceRecordSize.claim.check.columns.include.list=inventory[.]customers[.]payload transforms.EnforceRecordSize.claim.check.storage.class=io.debezium.storage.s3.S3OversizedRecordStorage transforms.EnforceRecordSize.claim.check.storage.base.path=s3://my-bucket/debezium/oversized transforms.EnforceRecordSize.claim.check.storage.region=us-west-1

The debezium-storage-s3 artifact must be on the same plugin path as the connector. Debezium never deletes stored objects, so configure a retention policy, such as an S3 lifecycle rule, to expire them once consumers no longer need them. (dbz#2379)

Signal data collection is validated up front

The signal.data.collection setting is now validated when the connector configuration is validated, for the MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and MongoDB connectors. Misconfigurations are reported immediately rather than surfacing later when a signal is sent.

The validation checks that the table or collection exists and that the value uses the form the connector expects. If the form is wrong, the error message names the exact value to use instead. For relational connectors, it also checks that the table resolves to at least three columns after column filters are applied. (dbz#2633)

New StringifyFields transformation

Some sinks store flexible data in JSON text columns and reject native struct, array, or map values. Examples include Databricks Delta VARIANT columns and PostgreSQL JSON and JSONB columns.

The new StringifyFields transformation serializes selected fields to JSON strings and changes their type to STRING, while the rest of the record stays strongly typed. Fields can be addressed by a dot path, such as after.payload, which makes it easy to handle nested data, for example after a MongoDB document is flattened with ExtractNewDocumentState.

The following example serializes the nested payload field in a change event:

transforms=stringify transforms.stringify.type=io.debezium.transforms.StringifyFields transforms.stringify.fields=after.payload,before.payload

Because the before and after fields share the same schema, a nested path inside the envelope must be listed under both. For a top-level field, such as one produced by a flattening transformation, list the field name on its own, for example fields=properties. (dbz#2903)

Debezium for MongoDB

Resume tokens in event source metadata

MongoDB change events now include an optional source.resume_token field that contains the full resume token as a JSON string, formatted according to the json.serialization.mode setting. Consumers can use this token with MongoDB’s resumeAfter to pick up a change stream from a specific event.

The token is only present for streaming events, and snapshot records carry a null value. For split events that are reassembled, the token of the final fragment is exposed. (dbz#718)

Readable starting timestamps

Starting capture from a point in time previously required capture.start.op.time, which expects a packed 64-bit BSON timestamp that is easy to confuse with a Unix timestamp.

The new capture.start.timestamp property accepts readable values instead, including Unix seconds, ISO-8601 timestamps such as 2026-09-11T00:00:00Z, and BSON Timestamp Extended JSON. It applies when the connector starts without a stored offset, and stored offsets still take precedence. MongoDB must still retain the requested position in the oplog. (dbz#2610)

Independent and required pre- and post-image policies

The MongoDB connector previously requested pre- and post-images with MongoDB’s whenAvailable policy, so a missing image went unnoticed. For workloads that depend on complete document states, this could silently produce incomplete events.

Pre- and post-images are now configured independently with two new properties, and each one can be marked as required. When a required image is unavailable, for example because image recording was disabled on a collection or the retained images expired, the connector fails visibly instead of emitting an incomplete event.

Property Value Behavior

capture.mode.pre.image

off (default)

Pre-images are not requested.

when_available

Pre-images are included when MongoDB has them.

required

The connector fails if a pre-image is unavailable.

capture.mode.post.image

off

Update events do not include the full document.

lookup (default)

The full document is retrieved with a separate lookup.

post_image

Post-images are included when MongoDB has them.

post_image_required

The connector fails if a post-image is unavailable.

For example, the following configuration requires both images:

capture.mode.pre.image=required capture.mode.post.image=post_image_required

Images must be enabled on the captured collections with changeStreamPreAndPostImages, which requires MongoDB 6.0 or later.

With these new properties, capture.mode and capture.mode.full.update.type are now deprecated. Existing configurations keep working and map to the new properties as follows:

capture.mode Pre-image Post-image

Not set

off

lookup

The capture.mode.full.update.type property defaults to lookup. If you set either new property explicitly, including to off, it takes precedence over the deprecated settings for that image only. (dbz#2688)

query.fetch.size applies to change streams

The query.fetch.size property is now honored when opening MongoDB change streams, letting you tune how many change stream documents are fetched per server response. This setting is independent of snapshot.fetch.size and max.batch.size.

When the property is omitted or set to 0, the connector keeps its current behavior and lets the driver decide. (dbz#2690)

Lower latency after idle periods

When the connector’s internal buffer was empty, the streaming consumer slept between polls, so an event arriving during that sleep waited until the sleep finished.

The consumer is now woken as soon as a buffered event becomes available, reducing latency for events that arrive after an idle period. (dbz#2754)

Required images work with regex collection filters

With a required image policy, the connector previously failed when an excluded collection without image recording changed, as long as it was within the change stream scope. This affected the default filters.match.mode=regex with capture.scope set to deployment or database.

Excluded collections are now filtered out before MongoDB looks up images, so only the collections you capture need image recording enabled. (dbz#2881)

Debezium for MySQL

Schema from binlog metadata without a schema history topic

When the server runs with binlog_row_metadata=FULL, available in MySQL 8.0 and later and MariaDB 10.5 and later, every binlog event carries complete column metadata for the table it changes.

The new opt-in binlog.metadata.based.schema property lets the MySQL and MariaDB connectors rebuild table schemas directly from that metadata. When enabled, the connector no longer needs a schema history topic, which removes the bootstrap, recovery, and operational overhead of managing one. The connector fails fast at startup if binlog_row_metadata is not set to FULL. (dbz#978)

Debezium for Oracle

Column reselection uses the physical standby

When the connector is configured with capture.mode=physical_standby, the ReselectColumnsPostProcessor now automatically queries the standby database through the secondary connection. Previously, reselection queries always went to the primary database, even though the connector was otherwise reading from the standby.

No additional configuration is needed, and this keeps reselection load off the primary. Other capture modes continue to query the primary database as before. (dbz#2444)

Faster transaction cache event counting

The transaction cache previously recomputed the count of all events across all transactions every time an event was processed, which took a noticeable share of event processing time. It now keeps a running count, removing that overhead from the hot path. (dbz#2777)

Faster eldest transaction lookup

Finding the eldest transaction in the cache runs on every commit. Its implementation has been streamlined, which improves throughput for workloads with many interleaved transactions that each contain only a few events. (dbz#2780)

Heartbeats for quiet tables with unbuffered LogMiner

With the unbuffered LogMiner adapter, the connector did not emit periodic heartbeats when the captured tables received no changes, even though the database itself remained active. As a result, the connector’s offset could not advance.

Unbuffered LogMiner now emits heartbeats on quiet streams just like the buffered adapter, so the safe recovery position can be checkpointed as it advances. (dbz#2781)

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Text array column defaults

Adding a text[] or varchar[] column with a default value, such as DEFAULT '{}', previously dropped the default from the generated schema. This broke Avro and Schema Registry compatibility checks and could stop the connector.

Default values for these array columns are now parsed and included in the schema. (dbz#1269)

Faster pgoutput string decoding

String decoding for pgoutput messages has been optimized to avoid unnecessary copies and allocations. Benchmarks show roughly 1.4 to 2 times higher throughput for the length-prefixed strings found on the hot path, and up to 4.6 times for null-terminated strings, while also reducing garbage collection pressure. (dbz#2710)

Debezium for SQL Server

Non-blocking reads from CDC tables

Queries that read directly from SQL Server CDC tables now use WITH (NOLOCK). This keeps Debezium’s reads from blocking the SQL Server capture job or production workloads.

This follows Microsoft’s guidance for CDC. Because CDC change tables contain only committed, insert-only data, these reads cannot see uncommitted changes. (dbz#2334)

Faster change timestamps in function query mode

In the default data.query.mode=function, the change query computed each row’s commit timestamp by calling a SQL Server function once per row. Function mode now resolves timestamps the same way as direct mode already does, avoiding the per-row function cost on high-volume tables without changing which rows are returned. (dbz#2693)

Debug logging of captured CDC tables

The connector already logged CDC-enabled tables that were excluded by its filters, but nothing listed the tables it actually captures. It now logs the CDC-enabled tables on the include list at DEBUG level, which makes it easier to troubleshoot why a table isn’t being captured. (dbz#2712)

Debezium JDBC sink

Resilient schema evolution with multiple tasks

When several sink tasks consumed from a multi-partition topic with schema evolution enabled, they could all try to add the same missing column at once. The first task succeeded, while the others failed with a "column already exists" error and stopped.

The sink now handles this race gracefully, so tasks keep processing records instead of failing. (dbz#2302)

Shared Sink Framework is now the default

The JDBC sink connector now uses the Shared Sink Framework by default. The framework adds a common buffering and batch processing layer, which deduplicates records by primary key within a batch and can route failing records to the Kafka Connect errant record reporter. Documentation for the new configuration options has been added as well.

The new buffer.mode property controls how records with the same key are handled within a batch, and it replaces the deprecated use.reduction.buffer property, which no longer has any effect. Its default is deduplication, which keeps only the most recent event for each key, similar to enabling the old reduction buffer. If you did not previously set use.reduction.buffer=true, set buffer.mode=passthrough to keep the same behavior as before, where every change event is written to the database:

buffer.mode=passthrough

If you run into problems with the new mode, you can switch the connector back to the legacy mode with the following setting:

internal.enable.sces=false

If you need to fall back, please let us know about the problem so we can address it. (dbz#2512)

MULTIPOLYGON support for SingleStore

The SingleStore JDBC sink previously rejected MULTIPOLYGON values, so spatial data from sources such as PostGIS could not be written to a SingleStore GEOGRAPHY column. These values are now converted to SingleStore’s POLYGON representation, which can describe multiple regions and holes. (dbz#2880)

Optional polygon repair for SingleStore

SingleStore limits coordinates to eight decimal places and validates polygons on insert, so some source geometries are rejected after rounding or because they self-intersect. In one migration, about 8% of records failed for this reason.

The new dialect.singlestore.geometry.repair.enabled option, disabled by default, rounds coordinates and repairs invalid polygons before writing them. Repair may change boundaries, holes, or regions, so enable it only when that tradeoff is acceptable. (dbz#2909)

Debezium Elasticsearch sink

New Elasticsearch sink connector

Debezium now includes a sink connector for Elasticsearch that consumes events from Kafka topics and writes them as documents to Elasticsearch indices. It works with native Debezium change events, flattened events, and plain structured events, and it preserves the meaning of Debezium’s logical types. For example, decimals are written as numbers, temporal values as ISO-8601 strings, JSON columns as embedded objects, geometry as GeoJSON, and vectors as arrays.

Every write and delete is addressed by a stable document ID, derived from the record key by default. If an event is delivered more than once after a restart or rebalance, it updates the same document rather than creating a duplicate. The connector supports Elasticsearch 8.x and 9.x clusters, while OpenSearch and other forks are not supported.

The connector runs in Kafka Connect, and Debezium Server also includes it as a built-in elasticsearch sink. The following examples show a basic configuration for each:

Kafka Connect
{ "name": "elasticsearch-connector", "config": { "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.elasticsearch.ElasticsearchSinkConnector", "tasks.max": "1", "connection.url": "https://elasticsearch:9200", "connection.auth.mode": "basic", "connection.username": "elastic", "connection.password": "changeme", "topics": "inventory.customers", "collection.name.format": "customers", "write.method": "upsert", "primary.key.mode": "record_key", "mapping.mode": "create_if_absent" } }
Debezium Server
debezium.sink.type=elasticsearch debezium.sink.elasticsearch.connection.url=https://elasticsearch:9200 debezium.sink.elasticsearch.connection.auth.mode=basic debezium.sink.elasticsearch.connection.username=elastic debezium.sink.elasticsearch.connection.password=changeme debezium.sink.elasticsearch.write.method=upsert debezium.sink.elasticsearch.primary.key.mode=record_key

In Debezium Server, any connector property can be set with the debezium.sink.elasticsearch. prefix. The dead letter queue is a Kafka Connect feature, so in Debezium Server a record that Elasticsearch rejects stops the server instead, ensuring no event is committed past a failed write.

The connector is currently incubating, so we encourage you to try it out and share your feedback, but it is not yet recommended for production use. Configuration properties, defaults, and behavior may change in future releases. (dbz#819)

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Debezium components as CDI beans

Debezium normally creates pluggable components, such as topic naming strategies, post-processors, and custom converters, from class names in the configuration or through Java’s ServiceLoader. In a Quarkus application, you can now define these components as CDI beans instead, so they can take part in dependency injection like the rest of your application.

When the Debezium Engine Quarkus extension finds a bean of a supported type, it uses that bean automatically, with no additional configuration. If a class is also configured for the same component, such as topic.naming.strategy, the bean takes precedence. Supported types include TopicNamingStrategy, PostProcessor, CustomConverter, HeartbeatFactory, SchemaHistory, and TransactionMetadataFactory.

For example, the following bean adds a custom prefix to every topic name:

PrefixTopicNamingStrategy.java
@ApplicationScoped public class PrefixTopicNamingStrategy implements TopicNamingStrategy<DataCollectionId> { @Override public void configure(Properties props) { } @Override public String dataChangeTopic(DataCollectionId id) { return "inventory." + id.identifier(); } @Override public String schemaChangeTopic() { return "inventory.schema-changes"; } @Override public String heartbeatTopic() { return "inventory.heartbeat"; } @Override public String transactionTopic() { return "inventory.transaction"; } @Override public String sanitizedTopicName(String topicName) { return topicName; } }

When your application runs more than one engine, annotate the bean with @Engine("<engine-id>") to apply it to a single engine. A bean with the @Engine annotation takes precedence over a bean without one, which applies to all engines. (dbz#1349)

Debezium Platform

Snapshot progress monitoring

Debezium Platform can now show the progress of initial and incremental snapshots. (dbz#2536)

Duplicate an existing transform

Creating a transform similar to an existing one previously meant re-entering its class, configuration, and predicate. You can now duplicate a transform, which opens the create form pre-filled with a unique name, while the original stays unchanged.

In the pipeline designer, you can either reuse an existing transform or create a copy that is attached only to the current pipeline. (dbz#2644)

Duplicating an existing transform

Snapshot progress on Overview and a new Snapshots tab

The pipeline overview page now shows a snapshot card while a snapshot is running, with the snapshot type, overall progress, completed tables, and elapsed time.

A new Snapshots tab in the pipeline details page shows a per-table breakdown with status, progress, and rows scanned, along with the reason for any skipped or failed tables. Progress updates are streamed live, and a badge appears on the tab while a snapshot is active. (dbz#2724)

Snapshot progress on the Overview and Snapshots tab

Host deployment example

A new runnable example in Debezium Examples demonstrates host-based pipeline deployment on a Linux VM. It walks through letting Conductor discover and provision the VM, creating a PostgreSQL to HTTP pipeline, and verifying a change event end to end. (dbz#2855)

Debezium Server

NATS offset and schema history storage

A new debezium-storage-nats module lets Debezium store connector offsets and schema history in NATS JetStream. If you already use NATS, for example as a Debezium Server sink, you can keep Debezium’s state there too, without running Kafka or another storage service.

Offsets are stored in a NATS Object Store bucket, and schema history is stored in a JetStream stream. Multiple connectors can share the same offset bucket, and the schema history stream is created automatically if it does not exist.

The following example configures both stores:

offset.storage=io.debezium.storage.nats.offset.NatsOffsetBackingStore offset.storage.nats.url=nats://localhost:4222 offset.storage.nats.bucket.name=debezium-offsets schema.history.internal=io.debezium.storage.nats.history.NatsSchemaHistory schema.history.internal.nats.url=nats://localhost:4222 schema.history.internal.nats.stream.name=debezium-schema-history schema.history.internal.nats.subject=debezium.schema.history

In Debezium Server, prefix these properties with debezium.source.. The debezium-storage-nats artifact must be on the classpath, and both stores support user and password or token authentication, as well as TLS. (dbz#1079)

Debezium for Spanner

Change streams for placement tables

The Spanner connector now supports change streams for placement tables. (dbz#1415)

Debezium for YashanDB

Advanced YStream client options

The YashanDB connector previously exposed only a subset of the YStream client’s options, so using any other option required a new connector release.

The new ystream.additional.properties setting accepts a list of name=value entries that are passed to the YStream client, and a dedicated ystream.fault.tolerance property has been added. Dedicated connector properties take precedence when both configure the same option, and invalid entries are rejected with a clear error. (dbz#2861)

Container Images

Fedora 44 base image

The Debezium container images have been upgraded to the Fedora 44 base image. (dbz#2774)

Debezium Examples

JBang and Hardwood Parquet example

A new example shows how to build a CDC pipeline with a single JBang script that uses the Debezium Quarkus extension and Hardwood. It captures snapshot events from PostgreSQL and writes them to Apache Parquet files. You can find the example in the debezium-examples repository. (dbz#2963)

item.content:encoded:
Google Summer of Code 2026 with the Debezium community was the best learning experience I have had as an engineer. Over one summer I built a Kafka Connect source connector from scratch for a database with no documented way to read its changes. Most of the work was taking the database apart to find out where those changes live, writing the design down before building any of it, and carrying each piece through review with the Debezium maintainers. The connector shipped in Debezium 3.7.

What came out of that summer is a Debezium source connector that turns Milvus, the open source vector database, into a first-class source of change events. I built it because Milvus has no change stream of its own. If you need its inserts and deletes somewhere else (Elasticsearch for keyword search, Redis as a cache, Postgres for reporting), you either write to both systems from the application and drift apart on the first partial failure, or you run a batch export that cannot see a delete. The connector reads the write stream Milvus already publishes to its message queue, puts the events back in commit order, and emits each insert and delete as a normal Debezium change event with the vector as a typed field. From there any Kafka Connect sink is a Milvus integration, and the service that writes to Milvus never has to know. This post covers how it works and what you can build once Milvus is one.

I built the connector against Milvus 2.5, which publishes every write to Kafka. Three factors drove the choice of 2.5:

  • The 2.6 version is still evolving in 2026 and has some breaking changes,

  • The only existing reference implementation, Zilliz’s milvus-cdc, reads the 2.5 message queue,

  • The majority of production deployments were on 2.5.

Consequently, I designed the connector to consume from Kafka and placed the transport layer behind an abstraction, rather than embedding Kafka directly into the connector. This design ensures that all components above the transport layer including the deserializer, timetick ordering engine, schema layer, dispatcher, and offset management are transport-agnostic. They operate on a MilvusMessageConsumer interface and RawMilvusMessage type, without any direct knowledge of Kafka ConsumerRecord. Adapting the connector for Milvus 2.6 would then only require implementing a Woodpecker-specific version of this interface and a corresponding WAL offset type, leaving the rest of the pipeline unchanged.

What is Milvus

A vector database stores embeddings (the high-dimensional float arrays that machine-learning models produce to represent text, images, or audio) and answers nearest-neighbor queries over them. Relational and keyword-search databases are built around exact matches and B-tree or inverted-index lookups, not approximate similarity search.

Milvus is an open source vector database built for that workload. Zilliz open-sourced it in 2019. It underpins semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendation systems, multimodal search, and deduplication and similarity pipelines.

Milvus 2.5 separates storage from compute:

  • Stateless proxies take requests,

  • The root, data and query coordinators own metadata and timestamps,

  • Query nodes serve searches and data nodes build segments,

  • The storage layer is etcd for metadata, MinIO or S3 for segment files, and a log broker (Pulsar, Kafka or RocksMQ) for the write stream.

Every insert and delete is appended to it first, and the data nodes and query nodes are subscribers that apply the log. Milvus 2.6 replaces the external broker with its own WAL, Woodpecker, which is the version split described at the top of this post. The connector reads the broker and etcd directly, so it needs a self-hosted Standalone or Distributed deployment with Kafka as the broker. Milvus Lite, the embedded Python library, has no broker to read.

Once Milvus holds production data, a second problem shows up that has nothing to do with vector search: everything around Milvus needs to know when that data changes.

Event-Driven Vector Architectures

Once Milvus becomes a live system of record for embeddings, it stops being the end of your data pipeline and becomes the middle of it. Downstream systems need its inserts and deletes as events:

  • A keyword-search mirror (Elasticsearch) that must never drift from the collection,

  • A cache or companion store (Redis) serving payloads next to ANN results,

  • Analytics pipelines counting what was added and removed,

  • Backup and compliance systems that need a durable record of every deletion.

Teams solve this today with two patterns, and both fail in well-understood ways. Dual writes (the application writes to both Milvus and Elasticsearch or Redis) desynchronize on the first partial failure, and there is no way to reconcile because neither side knows which write was the truth. Batch export cannot see deletes at all because by the time the export job runs, the row is already gone from Milvus, so the downstream copy keeps serving data the source deleted. Milvus’s query_iterator is one-shot. It can copy a collection, but it cannot follow one.

The Milvus maintainers describe this gap themselves:

  • In discussion #36683, a user who needed to export ~1M records from Milvus to Elasticsearch had hand-rolled a batch Java tool. The maintainers conceded that query_iterator was the only way to export readable data from Milvus and pointed to CDC for incremental export to Kafka.

  • In discussion #17088, maintainers confirmed that a change-subscription interface was still in progress.

  • Zilliz built a dedicated CDC daemon, milvus-cdc, for active-standby disaster recovery, but it can only sink into another Milvus.

The alternative is an event-driven vector architecture: Milvus stays the source of truth for embeddings, its commit stream is published to Kafka as ordered change events, and any number of consumers subscribe independently. Adding a consumer changes nothing in the source system.

Why a Milvus Source Connector

Milvus exposes no change stream over its gRPC API, so something has to bridge its internals to Kafka. A Debezium source connector is the natural shape for that bridge, because Debezium brings the CDC machinery for free:

  • A snapshot + streaming model, with the handoff between them anchored to a Milvus checkpoint.

  • Ordered delivery and Kafka Connect’s standard offset management, so restarts resume from a persisted position instead of from scratch.

  • The standard Debezium change-event envelope (before/after/source/op), which means every existing single message transform and converter in the Debezium ecosystem works unchanged.

  • The entire Kafka Connect sink ecosystem. Once Milvus changes are Debezium events on a topic, the Elasticsearch sink, the Redis sink, the S3 sink, and the JDBC sink are all Milvus integrations, with zero custom code. This is what generalizes the milvus-cdc idea from replicating to another Milvus to replicating to anything.

Three things separate this connector from relational CDC:

  1. Vector-aware payloads. Float vectors are emitted as the io.debezium.data.FloatVector logical type, and JSON and geometry fields map to io.debezium.data.Json. Consumers see typed vectors, not opaque blobs.

  2. No WAL, no binlog. The connector’s starting point comes from a Milvus channel checkpoint stored in etcd. From there its position is an offset into Milvus’s message queue plus a timetick watermark per virtual channel.

  3. TSO ordering. Events are ordered by Milvus’s own timestamp oracle (TSO) using its timetick protocol.

Use Cases

  • Hybrid search with a keyword mirror. Vector search is weak at exact tokens such as SKUs or names, so teams pair Milvus with Elasticsearch or OpenSearch and fuse the rankings. The mirror is only correct if it holds exactly what the collection holds, deletions included. The Elasticsearch sink with the Milvus primary key as the document _id does that.

  • RAG freshness. In a retrieval-augmented system the events that matter are deletes and re-embeds: a document retracted, a chunk re-embedded under a new model. A consumer of the change stream can invalidate cached answers keyed on the affected chunk IDs, or record what the retriever could see at a given TSO so an answer can be audited later.

  • Deletion evidence for compliance. A right-to-erasure request is not closed until the embedding is gone too, and batch export cannot show a deletion at all. The connector emits an op=d with the key and commit timestamp, followed by a tombstone, and a JDBC or S3 sink keeps it as a durable record.

  • Migration and model rollouts. Moving to another store means running its sink until the counts match and flipping the readers. Rolling out a new embedding model means a consumer that re-embeds each insert into a second collection. When it has caught up, the retriever switches.

Why Migrate to the Connector

Anyone who needs Milvus changes downstream already has something in place, and the case depends on what that is.

  • From dual writes. The first partial failure leaves Milvus and the mirror disagreeing with no record of which write was the truth, and every new consumer is a code change in the ingestion service. With the connector the ingestion service writes Milvus alone, and a mirror is a sink registration.

  • From batch export. A scheduled query_iterator job cannot see deletes, lags by however often it runs, and scans the whole collection each time. The connector emits deletes, lags by about a second, and after the snapshot its only calls to Milvus are one DescribeCollection per new collection: streaming reads the message queue.

  • From milvus-cdc. Zilliz’s daemon is the right tool for active-standby replication into a second Milvus and is more mature than this connector, but another Milvus is the only sink it has. Keep it for disaster recovery. The connector is for everything that is not another Milvus.

  • From a hand-rolled channel reader. Consuming the pchannel directly means owning two undocumented wire formats, the timetick watermark, the delete-before-insert rule, the etcd checkpoint and offset persistence. That list is this connector.

The Complexity of Milvus

Most Debezium source connectors share one identity: the database keeps an ordered change log, exposes a documented interface to read it, and hands out a position to resume from. Milvus breaks every part of that, and what it does not provide the connector has to build.

  1. No change log to ask for. Other source connectors read a change log the database provides for the purpose: a replication slot, a binlog, change tables, a change stream. Milvus has no change API. Its write stream is an internal message-queue topic meant for its own data nodes, in two undocumented wire formats whose only specification is msg.proto.

  2. A Kafka topic as the write-ahead log. This is the first Debezium source connector whose source is a database’s internal Kafka topic, in the database’s own format, rather than an API or a CDC feed already shaped like Debezium events. That puts a Kafka consumer, with its own consumer group, poll loop and partition assignment, inside a Kafka Connect source task, against a cluster that may not be the one Connect runs on, and makes the connector’s resume position an offset on somebody else’s topic.

  3. Four systems where a relational connector has one. Another source connector opens one connection to one database. This connector’s source is a running combination of Milvus, etcd, MinIO and Kafka, and it talks to three of them: Kafka for the stream, etcd for the checkpoint, Milvus over gRPC for schemas. Each has its own authentication, failure modes and version drift, and a wrong value for any one yields a connector that runs and captures nothing. The wrong default checkpoint key in the current release is exactly that failure. Every test of the connector, unit tests aside, means standing all four up.

  4. Order is reconstructed, not preserved. A pchannel interleaves independent vchannels, so arrival order is not commit order. The connector reimplements Milvus’s timetick watermark to restore TSO order, adds a rule for events sharing a timestamp (delete before insert, or an upsert deletes the row downstream), and bounds how long it waits for a quiet vchannel.

  5. No point to pin the snapshot to. Other source connectors snapshot inside a transaction pinned to a log position. Milvus’s query API cannot answer a query as of a given TSO, so the seam between snapshot and stream is at-least-once by construction, and idempotent, key-addressed sinks are part of the design.

Dissecting Milvus and the Debezium Connector

The Milvus write path, and why the connector taps the message queue

Milvus publishes every write to an internal message queue before it persists it. When a client calls insert, upsert, or delete over gRPC, the proxy validates the request and produces messages onto a physical channel (pchannel), a topic on Milvus’s MQ backend. Milvus’s own data nodes are consumers of that channel. Consuming it is how Milvus builds its segments and applies deletes.

So the connector does what Milvus’s own components do: it becomes another consumer of the pchannel. Zilliz’s milvus-cdc reads the same MQ. The consequence is that capturing changes requires access to three Milvus components, not one.

  1. The MQ backend (Kafka). The connector subscribes to the pchannel topic (milvus.pchannel.name, e.g. by-dev-rootcoord-dml_0) and consumes the raw insert, delete, and timetick messages Milvus writes there. These come in two wire formats, msgpack batches and single protobuf messages, and neither is documented. The schema lives in msg.proto.

  2. etcd. Milvus stores the per-channel checkpoint (a TSO and the MQ offset it had consumed up to) in etcd and does not expose it through any API, which is why the connector needs direct etcd access. This checkpoint is where streaming starts once the snapshot is done.

  3. The Milvus gRPC API. Used during the snapshot to list collections, read schemas, and query rows, and during streaming the first time a collection shows up on the channel: to resolve its primary key, and to fetch its whole schema if that first event is a delete.

An alternative design, polling collections through the API and diffing, was never seriously on the table: it cannot see deletes (the defining failure of batch export) and it cannot recover ordering. Reading the commit stream is more invasive infrastructurally (three endpoints instead of one), but it is the only design that observes what Milvus actually did, in the order it did it.

How collections are discovered

The connector does not require collections to be declared up front, which matters when collections are created per tenant or per model version and come and go.

  • During the snapshot, the connector lists collections through the Milvus metadata API, filters them against milvus.collection.include.list / exclude.list (literal names or Java regular expressions), and reads each schema.

  • During streaming, a collection is registered when its first event arrives on the pchannel. The raw insert message carries typed column data, which is enough to build the Connect schema. One DescribeCollection call over gRPC resolves the primary key (with a name-and-type heuristic as fallback), and if the first event is a delete, the whole schema comes from that call. The include and exclude lists are not consulted on this path: today every collection on the pchannel is streamed (see Limitations).

Each captured collection gets its own topic, named <topic.prefix>.<database>.<collection>. Note the database segment: the topic is milvus.default.products, not milvus.products. A sink configured with the short name finds no topic.

The snapshot and the handoff

The classic CDC failure mode sits at the seam between copying the existing data and streaming the new data: lose an event in the gap and the mirror is silently incomplete, or overlap them carelessly and you resurrect a deleted row. The connector’s answer is to anchor the stream at a point the snapshot is guaranteed to cover, the etcd checkpoint.

The snapshot starts by reading the channel checkpoint from etcd. That checkpoint pairs two values, a TSO and the MQ offset Milvus had consumed up to at that timestamp, and the connector keeps both. From there it:

  • Queries each included collection over gRPC with consistency_level=Strong, which makes Milvus answer with everything committed up to the query.

  • Emits every row it gets back as an op=r snapshot-read event stamped with the checkpoint TSO.

  • Records snapshot_completed = true in the connector offsets when the last collection has been read.

  • Seeks the MQ consumer to the message after the checkpoint offset, and

  • Begins streaming from there.

The order of those two reads is what makes the handoff safe. The checkpoint is taken before the query, so everything the checkpoint covers is inside the snapshot, and everything after it is in the stream the connector is about to read: nothing is lost. What the handoff does allow is overlap. A write that lands between the checkpoint and the snapshot query appears twice, once as op=r and again as op=c when the stream replays it, and insert.mode=upsert on the sink is what makes the second copy harmless. Milvus’s checkpoint trails its writes (by about a second in the run below), so seeded rows are exactly that case: in a run of the walkthrough’s example with the checkpoint path corrected, the four seeded rows came through as four reads followed by four creates. An earlier design pinned the query to the checkpoint TSO with guarantee_ts to close that window. The Milvus SDK’s query request has no such field, so the connector settles for at-least-once at the seam.

Milvus 2.5 stores that checkpoint under meta/datacoord-meta/channel-cp/<vchannel>, and the connector’s default looks under data-coord/checkpoint/binlog/channel/<pchannel>, a key that does not exist. Out of the box it therefore finds no checkpoint, logs a warning, snapshots anyway, and starts streaming from the end of the channel, which is why the snapshot event in the walkthrough carries "tso": 0. A write that lands between the snapshot query and that seek would be missed. Pointing milvus.etcd.checkpoint.path at the real key produces the behaviour described above (checkpoint found, stream resumed from the following offset, the overlap replayed and absorbed). Fixing the default is on the list at the end of this post.

Streaming, timeticks, and strict TSO order

Once streaming, the connector deserializes each raw MQ message, but arrival order on the pchannel is not commit order. Milvus multiplexes several virtual channels (vchannels) onto one pchannel, and each vchannel makes progress independently, so a message that arrives later may carry an earlier commit timestamp.

Milvus solves this internally with the timetick protocol, and the connector implements the same watermark logic in its timetick ordering engine:

  • Every event carries a TSO, a timestamp from Milvus’s central timestamp oracle, which defines the global commit order.

  • Each vchannel periodically publishes a timetick: a promise that it will never again produce an event older than that tick.

  • The engine buffers incoming events and maintains a global watermark, the minimum of the latest timeticks across all vchannels. Once the watermark reaches an event’s TSO, no vchannel can still produce anything older, so the event is released.

A four-message example shows the mechanism. Two vchannels, A and B, share one pchannel, and the connector reads, in arrival order:

  1. an event from A with TSO 105,

  2. an event from B with TSO 101,

  3. a timetick of 110 from A,

  4. a timetick of 108 from B.

The two events arrived in the wrong order, so the engine holds both in its buffer, sorted by TSO. Once both ticks are in, the watermark is the smaller of the two, 108, and every buffered event with a TSO at or below it is safe to release, because neither vchannel can produce anything older. The engine emits the event with TSO 101 and then the one with TSO 105, in strict TSO order, the reverse of how they arrived. An event with a TSO above 108 would stay buffered until a later round of ticks lifted the watermark past it.

Downstream consumers therefore observe changes in exactly the order Milvus committed them, across collections and across vchannels. Two decisions in that engine cost me the most to get right:

Deletes sort before inserts within one TSO. Milvus implements an upsert as a delete followed by an insert at a single TSO. Since the pair shares a timestamp, the engine must impose an order within the bucket, and it must be delete first: a consumer that applies insert-then-delete ends up with the row deleted after an upsert. An early version of the connector got this wrong, and no unit test noticed. The end-to-end demo did, when an upserted product vanished from Elasticsearch, the sink in an earlier iteration of the demo. (You’ll see the corrected pair, sharing one TSO, in the walkthrough.)

Liveness beats strictness under stall. The watermark only advances if every vchannel keeps ticking. If one goes quiet (a rebalance, an idle shard), strict ordering would buffer events forever. The milvus.timetick.stall.timeout.ms setting bounds this: once the watermark has not moved for that long (30 seconds by default) while events are waiting, the engine force-flushes what it has, logging that strict TSO ordering was relaxed, rather than halting the pipeline. It is a deliberate trade: strict ordering and roughly a second of commit-to-queryable latency on the healthy path, delivery instead of strictness when a channel goes silent.

Offsets: how progress is tracked

The connector’s offset (what Kafka Connect persists to resume from) is its position in Milvus’s message queue:

  • The Kafka offset of the last message read from the pchannel,

  • The latest timetick seen per vchannel,

  • The etcd checkpoint TSO the snapshot started from, and

  • The snapshot_completed flag.

One caveat sits in that list. The MQ position is advanced as messages are polled, before the events they carry have cleared the ordering buffer, and the offset attached to each emitted record is that latest polled position. If the connector crashes while events are still buffered, the restart seeks past them and they are lost. The window is short, the time events wait in the buffer, but it exists, so delivery is not strictly at-least-once in the current build. What is safe by construction is the snapshot: until snapshot_completed is committed, a restart re-runs it in full, which is why an idempotent, primary-key-addressed sink matters. One early demo run proved that point: crash-restarts duplicated the snapshot, producing 3,001 events on the topic for a 1,001-row collection, yet Elasticsearch converged to exactly 1,001 documents, because the Milvus PK was the ES document _id.

Walkthrough: Keeping Postgres (pgvector) in Sync with Milvus

Two services share one product corpus. An ingestion service owns writes: it embeds product data and inserts, upserts, and deletes rows in Milvus, the source of truth for the vectors and the engine that answers high-throughput ANN queries. Everything else about the business (orders, inventory, pricing, the reporting queries) already lives in Postgres, and the questions the back office asks are half vector, half relational: the ten products most similar to this one that are still in stock, which listings are near-duplicates of each other, how far apart two categories' embeddings are on average. With pgvector, each of those is a single SQL query with a join, provided the embeddings are in Postgres. Today they get there through a nightly batch copy that cannot see deletes, or not at all. The ingestion service should not know Postgres exists, and Postgres should hold the same vectors Milvus does, current to within a second.

The pipeline that delivers it is a Debezium source feeding a Debezium sink, with no transforms and no custom code anywhere.

Debezium already had the on-ramp to Milvus: the PostgreSQL connector captures pgvector columns as vector logical types, and Debezium Server ships a Milvus sink, so Postgres-to-Milvus is a configuration exercise. What was missing was the off-ramp: until now, vectors checked into Milvus and never checked out. That off-ramp is exactly what discussion #36683 asked for, an incremental export to Kafka.

What the connector takes responsibility for

That one event is small, but almost everything a CDC pipeline needs is already decided by the time it lands on the topic. The connector owns:

  • The snapshot and the handoff. It lists collections through the Milvus metadata API, pages through each one with consistency_level=Strong at milvus.snapshot.batch.size rows a time (1,000 by default, so a big collection never has to come back in one response), emits every row as op=r, then starts streaming from the etcd channel checkpoint and records snapshot_completed in its offsets, so a restart resumes instead of re-reading everything. snapshot.mode takes initial, never, recovery and when_needed.

  • Schema, without declarations. Collection schemas come from Milvus during the snapshot and from the first event while streaming, with one DescribeCollection call to resolve the primary key. Collections that appear later are picked up on their own.

  • Every Milvus field type, not only float vectors. Bool, the Int8 through Int64 family, Float and Double, VarChar and Text, Array, JSON and Geometry as io.debezium.data.Json, and the whole vector family: FloatVector as the typed logical vector in the event above, BinaryVector, Int8Vector, Float16Vector and BFloat16Vector as bytes, SparseFloatVector as JSON. decimal.handling.mode decides whether Float and Double arrive as floats, as Connect Decimal, or as strings. That FloatVector type name is what lets a generic JDBC sink create a pgvector column one step from now instead of a float array.

  • Identity. Every event is keyed by a Struct holding the Milvus primary key, which is what makes downstream idempotent: upsert on conflict, delete by key, replay safely.

  • Order. Events leave in strict Milvus TSO order across vchannels via the timetick watermark, with the delete ahead of the insert inside an upsert’s shared timestamp.

  • The Debezium envelope. before, after, source, op, plus tombstones after deletes, which means every existing Debezium SMT, converter and sink works against Milvus with no new code. Postgres is one sink file. Elasticsearch, Redis or S3 is a different sink file against the same topic, and Milvus never learns that a consumer was added.

  • Both Milvus wire formats. msgpack batches and single protobuf messages are both deserialized. If a message in the other format shows up, which is what a rolling Milvus upgrade produces, the task fails with a typed mismatch error naming the topic, partition and offset rather than a parse error with no address.

  • Bounded memory. The ordering buffer is capped by milvus.buffer.max.events (10,000) and milvus.buffer.max.bytes (64 MB). When it fills, the task stops polling the channel and drains whatever the watermark allows instead of growing until the JVM gives up.

  • Filtering and topic naming. Include and exclude lists take literal names or Java regular expressions and select collections (on the snapshot path today, see Limitations), and each collection gets its own topic, <prefix>.<database>.<collection>.

  • Talking to a real cluster. milvus.token for authenticated deployments, milvus.database to choose the database, and milvus.kafka.* for the consumer group, poll interval and partition the connector uses on Milvus’s MQ.

  • Operability. Pause, resume, restart and offset handling are plain Kafka Connect, with Milvus-specific metrics, heartbeats and Debezium notifications on top. The last section of the walkthrough exercises them.

One thing the registration does not mention is converters, and the example depends on the default. The Debezium Connect image runs JSON converters with schemas enabled, which is what gives the sink a Struct key to derive a primary key from and the FloatVector type name to act on. On a worker configured schemaless, set key.converter.schemas.enable=true and value.converter.schemas.enable=true on both connectors. The final output, in Postgres

sink-postgres.json is Debezium’s own JDBC sink.

  • primary.key.mode=record_key with primary.key.fields=pk makes the Milvus primary key the Postgres primary key. Every idempotency guarantee below follows from that one choice.

  • insert.mode=upsert and delete.enabled=true are the entire write path: op=r and op=c become INSERT …​ ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE, op=d becomes a DELETE by key, and the tombstone is understood.

  • schema.evolution=basic lets the sink issue the CREATE TABLE from the first event’s schema, which is where the FloatVector type name turns into a pgvector column.

  • collection.name.format=products names the table, because the default is the topic name, milvus.default.products, which is not valid SQL. (Debezium 3 renamed this setting, and table.name.format still works as a deprecated alias.)

And no transforms at all. A third-party sink needs transforms to unwrap the Debezium envelope and extract the key, plus settings that turn tombstones into deletes. The Elasticsearch version of this demo needed two. The Debezium JDBC sink reads Debezium envelopes natively, so its config is connection details and policy, nothing else.
