Both engines, one question

Everything so far would hold for any scalar table. The reason to pick pgvector is that the embedding arrived as a working vector, not an opaque payload, and the way to prove it is to ask both engines the same question. Take pk 1001’s embedding as the query, read back from Postgres as halfvec so that both sides are asked about the vector that made the round trip. Postgres ranks its three nearest neighbours by cosine distance (<⇒, the same metric the Milvus index was built with). Milvus answers the same query through its ANN search endpoint. Both return 1001, 1005, 1003, in that order.

Identical top-3 from a SQL ORDER BY and from Milvus’s ANN index, on vectors that travelled from Milvus through Kafka into Postgres as halfvec. The distances agree too: Postgres puts the camping stove at cosine distance 0.00915 from the running shoes, and Milvus reports a cosine similarity of 0.99085 for the same pair. From here, finding products similar to this one that are also in stock is a JOIN away.

Pause, write, resume

Finally, the offset guarantees when the connector stops. The README scripts this step with two rows written during the pause. The run below is a wider variant of it. Pause the source through the Connect REST API, insert three rows (a yoga mat, an espresso grinder, a board game) through the Milvus REST API while it is down, and resume. During the pause Milvus counts seven rows and Postgres still four. Within seconds of the resume Postgres counts seven as well, and the topic’s end offset stands at 13.

On resume, the topic replays exactly the three missed op=c events and the two counts match. Thirteen records in all:

  • Four snapshot reads,

  • One insert,

  • Three records for the upsert,

  • Two for the delete, and

  • Three rows written while the connector was paused.

No loss, no duplicates, on Kafka Connect offset management with no daemon involved.

For monitoring in production: The connector exposes snapshot and streaming metrics over JMX, where the standard MilliSecondsBehindSource is computed from the TSO watermark and the snapshot bean reports the checkpoint TSO it started from. Interval heartbeats (heartbeat.interval.ms) prove liveness on quiet collections.

Limitations and What’s Next

The connector is incubating. Its current limits, most serious first:

  • The default etcd checkpoint key does not match Milvus 2.5. The connector looks under a key that does not exist, so the snapshot runs without a checkpoint, streaming starts from the end of the channel, and a write that lands in between is missed. milvus.etcd.checkpoint.path can be pointed at the channel-cp key the handoff section names, but that key is per vchannel, so it covers one known collection at a time. The default needs fixing in the connector.

  • Streaming is not at-least-once across a crash. The MQ offset advances as messages are polled, before their events clear the ordering buffer, so a crash while events are buffered loses them on restart. The window is the time events wait in the buffer. The offsets section has the detail.

  • Kafka only, as Milvus’s MQ backend. The connector reads the MQ directly, so Pulsar and RocksMQ deployments are not supported, and neither is Milvus 2.6, which has no MQ.

  • Single task, single pchannel. One connector instance consumes one pchannel, and tasks.max values above 1 are ignored, so a Milvus deployment with more than one DML channel is only partly captured by one connector. The walkthrough configures Milvus with a single channel.

  • Include and exclude lists apply to the snapshot only. During streaming, every collection on the pchannel is captured.

  • No op=u events. A Milvus upsert surfaces as the delete+insert pair, not a synthesized update event. milvus.upsert.mode=correlate is accepted but nothing reads it yet, so it is a no-op.

  • PK-only before images on deletes. Milvus does not publish the prior state of a deleted entity, so the connector cannot either.

  • Collection DDL is not emitted. Create and drop operations are tracked for ordering but not emitted as schema-change events.

  • milvus.wire.format=auto picks the wrong format on an empty pchannel. If the connector is registered before any collection exists, the probe sees no data message and assumes msgpack_batch, and the first insert on Milvus 2.5 fails with a mismatch error. Set the format explicitly, as the walkthrough does, or restart the task once the channel has data.

Next on the list are the checkpoint default, upsert correlation behind milvus.upsert.mode=correlate, schema-change events for collection DDL, and replacing the wire format probe with detection from the first data message during streaming. Milvus 2.6 is the larger item and comes down to a Woodpecker implementation of the consumer interface from the dissection.

item.title: Alerting in the Debezium Platform
item.dc:creator: Indra Raj Shukla
item.description:
The Debezium Management Platform has been able to show you how your pipelines are doing for a while now. The monitoring dashboard tells you the event rate, the source lag, the queue utilization, whether the snapshot finished, and so on. But it is passive as it only helps while somebody is looking at it. In his mid-year Platform update, Mario listed alerting as one of the next things we wanted to tackle. That work has now landed.

The Platform can now watch those same panels for you and tell you when one of them crosses a line you care about. This post walks through what alerting looks like in the Platform, how a rule is defined, where notifications go, how an alert moves from quiet to firing, and where to review it all afterwards.

The Debezium Management Platform has been able to show you how your pipelines are doing for a while now. The monitoring dashboard tells you the event rate, the source lag, the queue utilization, whether the snapshot finished, and so on. But it is passive as it only helps while somebody is looking at it. In his mid-year Platform update, Mario listed alerting as one of the next things we wanted to tackle. That work has now landed.

The Platform can now watch those same panels for you and tell you when one of them crosses a line you care about. This post walks through what alerting looks like in the Platform, how a rule is defined, where notifications go, how an alert moves from quiet to firing, and where to review it all afterwards.

Quick recap of monitoring

Alerting is built on the monitoring panels, so it is worth recapping the path those numbers take.

A pipeline in the Platform is a Debezium Server instance deployed by the Debezium operator. The Platform wires it up with the OpenTelemetry Java Agent, which exports metrics over OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector. The collector re-exposes them in Prometheus format, Prometheus scrapes the collector, and the Conductor (Debezium Platform backend) queries Prometheus with PromQL when the UI asks for a panel.

For more details, take a look at the pipeline monitoring documentation.

Alerting

Rules apply a comparison and threshold to a monitoring panel. They evaluate globally, triggering a separate incident for each breaching pipeline, including those created later. You can find the full design in DDD-57: Alerting for Debezium Platform.

Anatomy of an alert rule

You will find a new Alerts section in the left navigation, with Rules, Channels and Events.

In the alert rule form, the fields read as a sentence:

When Source Lag (panel) Reduce last (how to collapse the time series) Is greater than 10 (comparison) For 5 minutes (how long it has to hold)

Read left to right, that is: when the last value of Source Lag is greater than 10 seconds for 5 minutes.

The pieces:

When: the monitoring panel, picked from a dropdown that groups panels into Streaming and Snapshot, exactly as on the monitoring tab.

Reduce: a panel is a time series, and a rule needs a single number. The reduce function decides how to get one: last, avg, min, max or sum. last is the default and is what you want for gauges like lag, connection status or queue utilization. avg is the better choice for noisy rate panels, where a single spike should not wake anybody up.

Evaluation window: how much history the reduce function looks at, from 1 minute to 1 hour, 5 minutes by default. It is ignored when reduce is last, and the form hides it in that case.

Is: the comparison, an operator such as greater than, with the threshold beside it. Once a panel is selected, its unit is shown next to the number, so a lag panel is entered in seconds and a utilization panel in percent.

For: the noise suppression knob, and the one worth getting right. The condition has to hold continuously for this long before the alert fires. Set it to Immediately and the slightest breach raises an alert, set it to 5 minutes and a transient blip resolves itself quietly.

Severity: Critical, Warning or Info. Severity is shown with both a colour and an icon rather than colour alone, and it determines whether the alert contributes to the badge in the header.

Additional channels: where to notify, on top of the UI itself.

A red dot in front of the name, as on pipeline-stalled in the screenshot above, means that rule has a firing incident. The status switch turns a rule off without deleting it, which is how you silence one during planned maintenance.

Where the notifications go

Alerts always appear in the Platform UI, so a freshly installed Platform gives you working alerting with no notification configuration at all. On top of that there are two more channel types, managed from Alerts → Channels:

Email: a list of recipients and an optional subject prefix.

Webhook: a URL, an HTTP method and optional headers, which is the integration point for Slack, PagerDuty, OpsGenie, Teams, or anything else that accepts a POST.

Channels are reusable: several rules can share one, and one rule can notify through several. Test, in the actions menu, sends a sample notification and reports back, so a bad SMTP setup shows up before a real incident does.

The webhook payload is intentionally flat and stable, with a version field so it can evolve without breaking your receiver:

{ "version": "1", "status": "firing", "alert": { "ruleName": "high-source-lag", "severity": "CRITICAL", "pipelineId": "inventory-pipeline", "value": 15.2, "threshold": 10.0, "message": "Source lag (15.2s) exceeded threshold (10.0s)", "firedAt": "2026-10-25T14:30:00Z" } }

The same shape is sent with "status": "resolved" when the incident closes, so a receiver can correlate the two.

The life of an alert

Saving a rule does not notify anyone by itself. Each time a pipeline crosses the line and comes back, that cycle is recorded as an incident.

From quiet to firing and back

The Platform runs an evaluation loop every 60 seconds by default. For each enabled rule it queries Prometheus, applies the reduce function, compares the result against the threshold for every pipeline reporting that metric, and moves that (rule, pipeline) pair through a small state machine:

Transition What happens

OK → Pending

The condition is met for the first time. Nothing is sent yet; the engine just remembers when it started.

Pending → OK

The condition cleared before the for duration elapsed. Silent reset, no notification. This is exactly what the for duration is there for.

Pending → Firing

The condition held for the whole for duration. An incident is created and notifications go out.

Firing → Resolved

The condition cleared. The incident is closed and a resolution notification goes out.

OK → Firing

Same as above but with for set to Immediately, skipping the pending state.

A firing alert sends one notification, and a resolution sends one. There is no repeat while it stays firing.

Alert events

The table lists each incident newest first. Expand a row for the value, the threshold and the message, and the pipeline name links to that pipeline’s monitoring dashboard. Filter by status or time range, and use Manage columns to choose which fields the table shows.

There is also a badge in the header, counting active Critical and Warning alerts across all pipelines. It takes the colour of the highest active severity: red when a Critical alert is firing, amber when the highest is a Warning. Clicking the badge opens this page filtered to firing incidents. Info alerts are recorded but left out of the badge.

A daily cleanup job removes resolved incidents older than the retention period, 30 days by default. Still-firing incidents are never purged, regardless of age.

Try it out

If you want to see it running end to end you can follow the platform monitoring and alert example in the debezium-examples repository. It brings up a local minikube cluster with PostgreSQL, Kafka, the OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus and the Platform, seeds a pipeline, and includes scripts that make the panels move by generating traffic, replaying a snapshot, and breaking the source connection.

From there, create a rule, trip it with one of those scripts, and watch it resolve.

Conclusion

Monitoring answered "how is my pipeline doing?" as long as you were looking. Alerting answers it when you are not.

Give it a try on the latest Platform images, and tell us which rules you end up writing.

If you like the project, you can help with feedback, report issues at issues, and add a star to the repository.

As always, feel free to leave a comment below or get in touch with us on the mailing list or in our Zulip chat.

item.content:encoded:
Hey community!

After a long period of development and testing, we are excited to announce that the sink framework is now the default in Debezium 3.8.0.Alpha1.

This framework introduces a new buffer and batch processing layer that lays the groundwork for a unified sink connector architecture across Debezium. It also provides a shared set of functionality for all sink connectors, such as key/payload mapping, filtering fields or collection name mapping.

What changed

Previous versions of the JDBC sink connector used a connector-specific buffering and write path. With 3.8.0.Alpha1, the sink framework is now enabled by default. This means all new deployments automatically benefit from the new batching and buffering behavior and other shared functionality that most sink connectors require.

The sink framework buffers incoming records and groups them into batches before writing them to the destination database. How records are buffered depends on whether a primary key is configured and which batch mode is selected.

When a primary key is configured, the connector tracks records by their key within the buffer. In deduplication mode (the default), if multiple records share the same key within a batch window, only the most recent record is kept. In passthrough mode, all events are preserved and the buffer is flushed whenever a duplicate key is encountered, so each individual batch contains no duplicate keys.

When you are upgrading and have used use.reduction.buffer property (even if you didn’t set it and used the default that changed with the new sink framework), you should now use the buffer.mode property instead. Mind that the default behavior has changed from passthrough to deduplication. And you need to set buffer.mode to passthrough if you want the old default behavior which processes every message/event.

When no primary key is configured, or when a record has a null key, each record receives a unique sequence number and both modes behave identically.

New configuration options

The sink framework introduces a few new configuration properties for the JDBC sink connector:

  • buffer.mode controls how keyed records are batched: deduplication (default, last-write-wins) or passthrough (preserves all events, splits batches at duplicate-key boundaries).

  • cloud.events.schema.name.pattern is a regular expression pattern to identify CloudEvents messages by their schema name (defaults to .\*CloudEvents\\.Envelope$).

For full details on these configuration options, see the JDBC sink connector documentation.

Switching back to the legacy mode

If you run into any severe issues with the new framework, you can switch back to the legacy buffering behavior by setting the following configuration property on your connector:

internal.enable.sces=false

This is an internal property and is intended as a temporary escape hatch. Our plan is to remove the legacy code path entirely once the sink framework has proven stable, likely with the Debezium 3.8.0.Final release.

Next steps

Currently we are finishing up the sink framework implementation for the MongoDB sink connector, with a planned release in Debezium 3.8.0.Final

We need your feedback

The sink framework is a significant architectural change, and we want to make sure it works well for everyone before we remove the legacy path. If you are using the JDBC sink connector, please try the 3.8.0.Alpha1 release and let us know how it goes.

If you encounter any issues, unexpected behavior, or performance differences compared to previous versions, please open an issue on Debezium GitHub or reach out on Zulip chat or the Debezium mailing list.

Your feedback is invaluable in helping us make the right call on when the legacy mode can be retired.

item.title: Debezium CLI: A Unified Command-Line Interface for CDC Pipeline Lifecycle Management
item.dc:creator: Binayak Das
item.description:
Change Data Capture (CDC) has established itself as the gold standard for real-time data streaming, cache invalidation, outbox pattern implementations, and microservice data synchronizations. For years, the Debezium project has empowered engineers worldwide to stream row-level database changes reliably into Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, Redis, and dozens of downstream cloud messaging platforms.

However, operating CDC pipelines traditionally came with operational friction. Developers had to hand-craft nested JSON connector configurations, deploy them via raw curl commands to Kafka Connect REST endpoints, navigate differing configuration dialects for standalone Debezium Server distributions, or manage complex Kubernetes manifests manually. With the introduction of the Debezium Platform, the ecosystem gained a robust control plane, but developers and platform engineers still needed a fast, intuitive, unified tool right in their terminal.

As part of Google Summer of Code (GSoC) 2026, we designed and built the Debezium CLI (debezium-jbang): a modern, zero-dependency command-line interface that covers the entire lifecycle of Debezium pipelines, from local scaffolding and daemonless container image assembly to real-time schema discovery and remote platform orchestration.

In this post, we explore the motivation, architecture, key capabilities, and hands-on workflows powered by the new Debezium CLI.

Why a Unified CLI?

The primary design principle behind Debezium CLI is developer velocity without infrastructure overhead. Whether an engineer is prototyping a new pipeline locally on their laptop or an SRE is auditing pipelines across multiple Kubernetes clusters, the CLI delivers:

  • Zero-Friction Installation: Powered by JBang, the CLI requires no manual Java compilation, package manager friction, or Maven installation. It runs everywhere Java or JBang is present, and supports instant execution via the Debezium catalog: jbang debezium@debezium.

  • Daemonless Distribution and Container Builds: Build custom Debezium Server distribution archives and layered OCI container images without needing a local Maven runtime or a running Docker daemon.

  • Unified Control Plane: Seamlessly manage connectors, transformations, destinations, and pipelines against Debezium Platform instances across development, staging, and production environments.

  • Live Discovery & Diagnostics: Discover database catalogs, validate connection credentials against live source databases, inspect schema collections, and stream runtime pipeline logs directly in the terminal.

Capabilities Overview

Under the hood, the Debezium CLI is built on Picocli and is organized into two primary, complementary subsystems:

Subsystem Commands Core Responsibilities

Build Subsystem

init, validate, build, push

Scaffolds dbz.yaml, performs static analysis, resolves Maven dependencies dynamically via Eclipse Aether, and builds layered OCI images via Google Jib Core without Docker.

Platform Subsystem

switch, config, catalog, source, destination, connection, transform, pipeline

Interfaces with the Debezium Platform REST API, providing multi-environment profiles, schema exploration, runtime health checks, and signal emission.

Getting Started

Getting started with the Debezium CLI takes less than thirty seconds.

Prerequisites

The Debezium CLI is distributed via JBang. If you don’t have JBang installed yet, you can install it on your system with a single command:

# macOS / Linux $ curl -Ls https://sh.jbang.dev | bash -s - app setup # Windows (PowerShell) $ iex "& { $(iwr -useb https://ps.jbang.dev) } app setup"

You can also use your preferred package manager (such as brew install jbangdev/tap/jbang or sdk install jbang). For other platforms and installation methods, see the official JBang installation guide.

Installation

With JBang installed, you can install the Debezium CLI globally from the official {prodname} catalog:

$ jbang app install debezium@debezium $ debezium --version

Alternatively, you can run commands directly on the fly without permanent installation:

$ jbang debezium@debezium --help

Once installed, explore all available commands using debezium --help.

Phase 1: Local Development & The Build Subsystem

The Build subsystem empowers developers to go from zero to a fully packaged, deployable Debezium Server container image in seconds, all governed by a declarative project descriptor: dbz.yaml.

1. Scaffolding a Project (init)

To scaffold a new CDC project, simply run debezium init specifying your source database and target sink:

$ debezium init --source postgres --sink kafka

This creates a templated dbz.yaml file pre-configured for your chosen source and sink:

# Debezium Server Configuration version: "1.0" debezium: version: "3.7.0.Alpha2" source: connector: "postgres" config: database.hostname: "${DBZ_DB_HOST:-localhost}" database.port: "${DBZ_DB_PORT:-5432}" database.user: "${DBZ_DB_USER}" database.password: "${DBZ_DB_PASS}" database.dbname: "${DBZ_DB_NAME:-inventory}" topic.prefix: "inventory" sink: type: "kafka" config: bootstrap.servers: "${DBZ_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP:-localhost:9092}" build: target: "tar" image: name: "debezium-server" registry: "ghcr.io/my-org" tag: "latest"

2. Static Analysis & Environment Validation (validate)

Before triggering any build, debezium validate verifies syntax, checks required fields, and audits referenced environment variables:

$ export DBZ_DB_USER=postgres $ export DBZ_DB_PASS=secretpassword $ debezium validate Project descriptor dbz.yaml is valid!

If a mandatory variable is missing, the validator alerts you before any resource is consumed.

3. Daemonless OCI Image Assembly (build)

Traditionally, building a custom Debezium Server container required writing a multi-stage Dockerfile, running a local Docker daemon, and downloading multi-gigabyte Maven dependency trees.

The Debezium CLI solves this using the Google Jib Core API and dynamic Eclipse Aether (Maven Resolver):

$ debezium build --image
Resolving dependencies for Debezium Server 3.7.0.Alpha2 (postgres -> kafka)... Resolved 48 artifacts (184 MB) in 4.2s. Assembling layered OCI image target/debezium-server.tar... [Layer 1/3] Base runtime: eclipse-temurin:21-jre-jammy [Layer 2/3] Debezium Server runtime libraries [Layer 3/3] User configurations and startup scripts Built OCI image archive: target/debezium-server.tar (image: debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest)

No Docker daemon required! The build runs inside CI runners, unprivileged Kubernetes pods, or developer laptops with equal fidelity.

4. Pushing to Container Registries (push)

Once the image tarball is assembled, debezium push publishes it directly to your target container registry:

# Push to Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry: $ debezium push --registry ghcr.io/my-org # Or push to a local/insecure development registry: $ debezium push --registry localhost:5001 --allow-insecure-registries
Pushing debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest -> localhost:5001... No credentials found — attempting anonymous push... Pushed: localhost:5001/debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest Pull with: docker pull localhost:5001/debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest

You can see the push workflow in action below:

Phase 2: Remote Orchestration & The Platform Subsystem

While the Build subsystem handles standalone packaging, modern architectures frequently rely on the Debezium Platform for centralized orchestration, dynamic reconfigurations, and centralized telemetry. The Debezium CLI provides native integration with the Platform API.

1. Multi-Environment Switching (config & switch)

Switching between development, testing, and production clusters is instant:

# Register and switch environments $ debezium config set --env=dev platform-url http://localhost:8080 $ debezium config set --env=staging platform-url https://platform.staging.internal:8080 $ debezium switch dev Switched to environment: dev $ debezium config get NAME URL ACTIVE ---- --- ------ dev http://localhost:8080 * staging https://platform.staging.internal:8080 Effective platform URL: http://localhost:8080

2. Discovering Connector Capabilities (catalog)

No need to browse documentation to find connector configuration properties. The CLI queries the live platform catalog directly:

$ debezium catalog list TYPE CLASS ------ -------------------------------------------------- source io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector source io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector $ debezium catalog get source io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
Name: Debezium PostgreSQL Connector Type: source-connector Version: 3.7.0-SNAPSHOT Description: Captures row-level changes from a PostgreSQL database in near real-time. NAME TYPE REQUIRED DEFAULT DESCRIPTION ----------------- ------ -------- ------- ----------- database.hostname string true Resolvable hostname or IP address. database.port number false 5432 Port of the database server. database.user string true Name of the database user.

JSON output is also supported via --format=json, making programmatic integration with CI/CD pipelines trivial.

3. Live Connection Validation & Database Discovery (connection)

Before creating a pipeline, the CLI lets you test your database credentials against the live network and inspect database schemas directly:

# Validate database connection parameters: $ debezium connection validate -f connection.yaml Connection is valid. # Discover schemas and tables in the target database: $ debezium connection collections 1 public public.customers public.orders public.order_lines public.products

4. Managing Pipelines & Sending Signals (pipeline)

Once sources and destinations are registered, creating and orchestrating pipelines takes a single command:

$ debezium pipeline create -f pipeline.yaml Pipeline created with id: 1 $ debezium pipeline list ID NAME SOURCE DESTINATION LOG LEVEL --- ---- ------ ----------- --------- 1 customer-sync pg-source kafka-dest INFO

Need to trigger an ad-hoc incremental snapshot or pause ingestion for maintenance? Use the pipeline signal command:

# Trigger an incremental snapshot: $ debezium pipeline signal --type=execute-snapshot \ --data='{"data-collections": ["public.customers"]}' 1 Signal sent to pipeline 1. # Adjust logging verbosity or pause ingestion: $ debezium pipeline signal --type=pause 1 Signal sent to pipeline 1.

What’s Next

While the Debezium CLI already covers core build and orchestration workflows in Debezium 3.7, several enhancements are planned for future releases:

  • Interactive Terminal User Interface (TUI): A rich, dynamic terminal dashboard for monitoring pipeline health, throughput rates, and event latencies in real time.

  • Operator Integration: Tighter bidirectional integration with the Debezium Kubernetes Operator for managing Custom Resources (DebeziumServer, etc.) directly from the CLI.

  • Consumer Lag and Health Diagnostics: Advanced diagnostics (debezium doctor) to audit database permissions, verify network reachability, and monitor consumer group lag.

  • Expanded Connector and Sink Templates: Additional scaffolding presets for emerging sources and sinks across the Debezium ecosystem.

Acknowledgements & GSoC 2026 Reflection

The Debezium CLI was designed and implemented during Google Summer of Code 2026.

A heartfelt and special thank you to my mentors, Giovanni Panice and Mario Fiore Vitale, for their invaluable guidance, detailed architectural feedback, and supportive code reviews throughout the program. Working alongside the Debezium core team has been an extraordinary learning journey in building resilient, enterprise-grade developer tooling for the open-source data streaming ecosystem.

We encourage everyone in the Debezium community to try out the new CLI, share feedback in the #community-platform channel on Zulip, and contribute ideas for upcoming releases!

# Debezium Server Configuration version: "1.0" debezium: version: "3.7.0.Alpha2" source: connector: "postgres" config: database.hostname: "${DBZ_DB_HOST:-localhost}" database.port: "${DBZ_DB_PORT:-5432}" database.user: "${DBZ_DB_USER}" database.password: "${DBZ_DB_PASS}" database.dbname: "${DBZ_DB_NAME:-inventory}" topic.prefix: "inventory" sink: type: "kafka" config: bootstrap.servers: "${DBZ_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP:-localhost:9092}" build: target: "tar" image: name: "debezium-server" registry: "ghcr.io/my-org" tag: "latest"

2. Static Analysis & Environment Validation (validate)

Before triggering any build, debezium validate verifies syntax, checks required fields, and audits referenced environment variables:

$ export DBZ_DB_USER=postgres $ export DBZ_DB_PASS=secretpassword $ debezium validate Project descriptor dbz.yaml is valid!

If a mandatory variable is missing, the validator alerts you before any resource is consumed.

3. Daemonless OCI Image Assembly (build)

Traditionally, building a custom Debezium Server container required writing a multi-stage Dockerfile, running a local Docker daemon, and downloading multi-gigabyte Maven dependency trees.

The Debezium CLI solves this using the Google Jib Core API and dynamic Eclipse Aether (Maven Resolver):

$ debezium build --image
Resolving dependencies for Debezium Server 3.7.0.Alpha2 (postgres -> kafka)... Resolved 48 artifacts (184 MB) in 4.2s. Assembling layered OCI image target/debezium-server.tar... [Layer 1/3] Base runtime: eclipse-temurin:21-jre-jammy [Layer 2/3] Debezium Server runtime libraries [Layer 3/3] User configurations and startup scripts Built OCI image archive: target/debezium-server.tar (image: debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest)

No Docker daemon required! The build runs inside CI runners, unprivileged Kubernetes pods, or developer laptops with equal fidelity.

4. Pushing to Container Registries (push)

Once the image tarball is assembled, debezium push publishes it directly to your target container registry:

# Push to Docker Hub or GitHub Container Registry: $ debezium push --registry ghcr.io/my-org # Or push to a local/insecure development registry: $ debezium push --registry localhost:5001 --allow-insecure-registries
Pushing debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest -> localhost:5001... No credentials found — attempting anonymous push... Pushed: localhost:5001/debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest Pull with: docker pull localhost:5001/debezium-server:postgres-kafka-latest

You can see the push workflow in action below:

Phase 2: Remote Orchestration & The Platform Subsystem

While the Build subsystem handles standalone packaging, modern architectures frequently rely on the Debezium Platform for centralized orchestration, dynamic reconfigurations, and centralized telemetry. The Debezium CLI provides native integration with the Platform API.

1. Multi-Environment Switching (config & switch)

Switching between development, testing, and production clusters is instant:

# Register and switch environments $ debezium config set --env=dev platform-url http://localhost:8080 $ debezium config set --env=staging platform-url https://platform.staging.internal:8080 $ debezium switch dev Switched to environment: dev $ debezium config get NAME URL ACTIVE ---- --- ------ dev http://localhost:8080 * staging https://platform.staging.internal:8080 Effective platform URL: http://localhost:8080

2. Discovering Connector Capabilities (catalog)

No need to browse documentation to find connector configuration properties. The CLI queries the live platform catalog directly:

$ debezium catalog list TYPE CLASS ------ -------------------------------------------------- source io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector source io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector $ debezium catalog get source io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector
Name: Debezium PostgreSQL Connector Type: source-connector Version: 3.7.0-SNAPSHOT Description: Captures row-level changes from a PostgreSQL database in near real-time. NAME TYPE REQUIRED DEFAULT DESCRIPTION ----------------- ------ -------- ------- ----------- database.hostname string true Resolvable hostname or IP address. database.port number false 5432 Port of the database server. database.user string true Name of the database user.

JSON output is also supported via --format=json, making programmatic integration with CI/CD pipelines trivial.

3. Live Connection Validation & Database Discovery (connection)

Before creating a pipeline, the CLI lets you test your database credentials against the live network and inspect database schemas directly:

# Validate database connection parameters: $ debezium connection validate -f connection.yaml Connection is valid. # Discover schemas and tables in the target database: $ debezium connection collections 1 public public.customers public.orders public.order_lines public.products

4. Managing Pipelines & Sending Signals (pipeline)

Once sources and destinations are registered, creating and orchestrating pipelines takes a single command:

$ debezium pipeline create -f pipeline.yaml Pipeline created with id: 1 $ debezium pipeline list ID NAME SOURCE DESTINATION LOG LEVEL --- ---- ------ ----------- --------- 1 customer-sync pg-source kafka-dest INFO

Need to trigger an ad-hoc incremental snapshot or pause ingestion for maintenance? Use the pipeline signal command:

# Trigger an incremental snapshot: $ debezium pipeline signal --type=execute-snapshot \ --data='{"data-collections": ["public.customers"]}' 1 Signal sent to pipeline 1. # Adjust logging verbosity or pause ingestion: $ debezium pipeline signal --type=pause 1 Signal sent to pipeline 1.

What’s Next

While the Debezium CLI already covers core build and orchestration workflows in Debezium 3.7, several enhancements are planned for future releases:

  • Interactive Terminal User Interface (TUI): A rich, dynamic terminal dashboard for monitoring pipeline health, throughput rates, and event latencies in real time.

  • Operator Integration: Tighter bidirectional integration with the Debezium Kubernetes Operator for managing Custom Resources (DebeziumServer, etc.) directly from the CLI.

  • Consumer Lag and Health Diagnostics: Advanced diagnostics (debezium doctor) to audit database permissions, verify network reachability, and monitor consumer group lag.

  • Expanded Connector and Sink Templates: Additional scaffolding presets for emerging sources and sinks across the Debezium ecosystem.

Acknowledgements & GSoC 2026 Reflection

The Debezium CLI was designed and implemented during Google Summer of Code 2026.

A heartfelt and special thank you to my mentors, Giovanni Panice and Mario Fiore Vitale, for their invaluable guidance, detailed architectural feedback, and supportive code reviews throughout the program. Working alongside the Debezium core team has been an extraordinary learning journey in building resilient, enterprise-grade developer tooling for the open-source data streaming ecosystem.

We encourage everyone in the Debezium community to try out the new CLI, share feedback in the #community-platform channel on Zulip, and contribute ideas for upcoming releases!

item.title: Native Support for Debezium in Apache Beam
item.dc:creator: Ilyas Ahsan
item.description:
Apache Beam has a built-in connector for Debezium called DebeziumIO. It lets you capture changes from your database and process them directly inside a Beam pipeline. You don’t need to run Apache Kafka or Kafka Connect.

item.content:encoded:
Apache Beam has a built-in connector for Debezium called DebeziumIO. It lets you capture changes from your database and process them directly inside a Beam pipeline. You don’t need to run Apache Kafka or Kafka Connect.

In this post, we’ll build an example pipeline that streams changes from MySQL into Google BigQuery. The complete example is available in the debezium-examples repository.

What is DebeziumIO?

DebeziumIO is a read connector in Apache Beam. It runs a Debezium connector inside your pipeline. Every time a row is inserted, updated, or deleted in your database, DebeziumIO turns that change into an event that the rest of your pipeline can use.

It is available in Apache Beam 2.76.0 and supports Debezium 3.5.

Because it is part of Beam, the pipeline can run on any Beam runner, for example:

  • Direct runner

  • Google Cloud Dataflow

  • Apache Flink

  • Apache Spark

Right now, it only supports these databases:

  • MySQL

  • PostgreSQL

  • SQL Server

  • Db2

DebeziumIO is still experimental, so there’s still room for improvement, and its API may change in future Beam releases.

Example Pipeline

graph LR subgraph S[Source System] DB[(MySQL)] end DB e1@-->|binlog / WAL| DC[DebeziumIO] subgraph BEAM[Apache Beam] DC e2@--> TS[Transform] TS e3@-->|TableRow| BI[BigQueryIO] end subgraph T[Target System] BQ[(BigQuery)] end BI e4@-->|sink| BQ e1@{ animate: true } e2@{ animate: true } e3@{ animate: true } e4@{ animate: true }

The example has only three parts:

  • Source: a MySQL database.

  • Pipeline: a Java application built with Apache Beam that uses DebeziumIO.

  • Destination: a Google BigQuery table.

Before you start

You need:

  • Java 17

  • Gradle

  • Docker

  • A Google Cloud project with BigQuery enabled

Just want to try it out? The apache-beam example starts MySQL and a BigQuery emulator with Docker Compose, so you don’t need a Google Cloud project. Follow the steps in its README.md to run the pipeline on your machine.

Start MySQL

We use the example MySQL image from the Debezium tutorial.

docker run -it --rm --name mysql -p 3306:3306 \ -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=debezium \ -e MYSQL_USER=mysqluser \ -e MYSQL_PASSWORD=mysqlpw \ quay.io/debezium/example-mysql:3.5.2.Final

Create BigQuery table

We need to create the BigQuery table first because the pipeline requires it to already exist.

CREATE TABLE my-project.my-dataset.customers ( metadata STRING, before STRING, after STRING, write_time NUMERIC );

Build the pipeline

Initialize Java Application

Create a new Java project with Gradle:

gradle init --type basic --dsl kotlin --project-name debeziumio-example --no-incubating

Then add the Debezium and Apache Beam dependencies to build.gradle.kts:

build.gradle.kts
plugins { java application } application { mainClass.set("org.example.Main") } val debeziumVersion = "3.5.2.Final" val beamVersion = "2.76.0" dependencies { // Debezium connector for MySQL implementation("io.debezium:debezium-connector-mysql:$debeziumVersion") // Apache Beam implementation("org.apache.beam:beam-sdks-java-core:$beamVersion") implementation("org.apache.beam:beam-sdks-java-io-debezium:$beamVersion") implementation("org.apache.beam:beam-sdks-java-io-google-cloud-platform:$beamVersion") implementation("org.apache.beam:beam-runners-google-cloud-dataflow-java:$beamVersion") runtimeOnly("org.apache.beam:beam-runners-direct-java:$beamVersion") }

The pipeline code goes in src/main/java/org/example/Main.java. The whole pipeline is a chain of three steps:

public static void main(String[] args) { Pipeline pipeline = Pipeline.create(PipelineOptionsFactory.fromArgs(args).withValidation().create()); pipeline .apply("ReadDatabaseEvents", ...) // Step 1: read change events from MySQL .apply("TransformToTableRow", ...) // Step 2: turn each event into a BigQuery row .apply("WriteToBigQuery", ...); // Step 3: write the rows to BigQuery pipeline.run(); }

Let’s look at each step.

Step 1: Read change events from MySQL

// Step 1. Read change events with Debezium .apply("ReadDatabaseEvents", DebeziumIO.readAsJson() .withConnectorConfiguration(ConnectorConfiguration.create() .withConnectorClass(MySqlConnector.class) .withHostName("localhost") .withPort("3306") .withUsername("debezium") .withPassword("dbz") .withConnectionProperty("database.server.id", "184054") .withConnectionProperty("database.include.list", "inventory") .withConnectionProperty("table.include.list", "inventory.customers") .withConnectionProperty("include.schema.changes", "false") .withConnectionProperty("snapshot.mode", "initial") .withConnectionProperty("snapshot.locking.mode", "none") .withConnectionProperty("tombstones.on.delete", "false") ) .withFormatFunction(new SourceRecordJson.SourceRecordJsonMapper()) .withCoder(StringUtf8Coder.of()) )

Here is what each setting does:

Setting What it does

database.server.id

A unique ID for this client. MySQL needs it to stream the binlog.

database.include.list

Only capture changes from these databases.

table.include.list

Only capture changes from these tables.

include.schema.changes

Don’t send events for schema changes (DDL). We only want data changes.

snapshot.mode

initial means: first read all existing rows, then stream new changes.

snapshot.locking.mode

none means: don’t lock tables during the snapshot. This helps on managed databases where the user is not allowed to lock tables. It is only safe if no schema changes happen while the snapshot runs.

tombstones.on.delete

Don’t send an extra empty "tombstone" event after each delete. Kafka uses tombstones to clean up old messages, and we don’t use Kafka here.

withFormatFunction(…​)

DebeziumIO needs a serializable function that turns each change event (a SourceRecord object) into something the pipeline can use. SourceRecordJsonMapper is a ready-made function that turns it into a JSON string.

withCoder(…​)

Tells Beam how to store the output. Our output is a string, so we use StringUtf8Coder.

Here is an example of the JSON string this step produces for an update:

{ "metadata": { "connector": "mysql", "version": "3.5.2.Final", "name": "beam-debezium-connector", "database": "inventory", "schema": "mysql-bin.000003", "table": "customers" }, "before": { "fields": { "id": 1001, "first_name": "Sally", "last_name": "Thomas", "email": "sally.thomas@acme.com" } }, "after": { "fields": { "id": 1001, "first_name": "Sally Anne", "last_name": "Thomas", "email": "sally.thomas@acme.com" } } }

Step 2: Turn each event into a BigQuery row

Next, we turn each JSON string into a BigQuery TableRow so it can be loaded into BigQuery. To keep things simple, we store metadata, before, and after as plain JSON strings. We also add a table_id field, which Step 3 uses to pick the target table.

This TableRow schema is simplified for the example. In a real project, adjust it to match your MySQL table schema.

 
// Step 2. Transform the records into TableRow .apply("TransformToTableRow", ParDo.of(new DoFn<String, TableRow>() { @ProcessElement public void processElement(ProcessContext c) throws IOException { JsonNode payload = new ObjectMapper().readTree(c.element()); TableRow record = new TableRow() .set("metadata", payload.get("metadata").toString()) .set("before", payload.get("before").toString()) .set("after", payload.get("after").toString()) .set("table_id", payload.get("metadata").get("table").asText()) .set("write_time", DateTimeUtils.currentTimeMillis()); c.output(record); } }))

Each change becomes one row, like this:

{ "metadata": "{\"connector\": \"mysql\", \"version\": \"3.5.2.Final\", \"name\": \"beam-debezium-connector\", \"database\": \"inventory\", \"schema\": \"mysql-bin.000003\", \"table\": \"customers\"}", "before": "{\"fields\": {\"id\": 1001, \"first_name\": \"Sally\", \"last_name\": \"Thomas\", \"email\": \"sally.thomas@acme.com\"}}", "after": "{\"fields\": {\"id\": 1001, \"first_name\": \"Sally Anne\", \"last_name\": \"Thomas\", \"email\": \"sally.thomas@acme.com\"}}", "table_id": "customers", "write_time": 1791790940612 }

The table_id field is only used to pick the target table. The BigQuery table has no table_id column, so ignoreUnknownValues() in Step 3 drops it when writing.

Step 3: Write the rows to BigQuery

Finally, we write each row to BigQuery.

// Step 3. Sink TableRow to BigQuery .apply("WriteToBigQuery", BigQueryIO.writeTableRows() .to((SerializableFunction<ValueInSingleWindow<TableRow>, TableDestination>) input -> { TableRow row = Objects.requireNonNull(Objects.requireNonNull(input).getValue()); TableReference tableReference = new TableReference() .setProjectId("my-project") .setDatasetId("my-dataset") .setTableId(row.get("table_id").toString()); return new TableDestination(tableReference, "Customer names and emails"); }) .withoutValidation() .ignoreUnknownValues() .withCreateDisposition(BigQueryIO.Write.CreateDisposition.CREATE_NEVER) .withWriteDisposition(BigQueryIO.Write.WriteDisposition.WRITE_APPEND) .withMethod(BigQueryIO.Write.Method.STREAMING_INSERTS))

Run the pipeline

Run on your machine

First, let your machine access Google Cloud:

gcloud auth application-default login

Then start the pipeline with the Direct runner:

./gradlew run --args="--runner=DirectRunner"

Run on Google Cloud Dataflow

To run the same pipeline on Dataflow, you only need to change the arguments:

./gradlew run --args="\ --runner=DataflowRunner \ --project=my-project \ --region=asia-southeast2 \ --streaming \ --experiments=enable_streaming_engine \ --jobName=debezium-mysql-to-bq \ --tempLocation=gs://my-bucket/temp \ --stagingLocation=gs://my-bucket/staging \ --numWorkers=1 \ --maxNumWorkers=1"

The result

Here is the pipeline in the Google Cloud Dataflow console. You can see the same three steps from our code: ReadDatabaseEvents, TransformToTableRow, and WriteToBigQuery.

In this run, the job reads from a MySQL database that the Dataflow workers can reach over the network. localhost only works with the Direct runner, so change withHostName(…​) in Step 1 to your database’s address when you run on Dataflow.

Once the job is running, the data from MySQL shows up in the BigQuery table:

This table uses the same columns as the MySQL customers table, as suggested in the note in Step 2. The data is also deduplicated by id, so each customer has only one row: the latest one, based on write_time.

Room for improvement

While building this example, I found a gap in DebeziumIO. Its metadata field keeps only some of the attributes from the Debezium source field:

DebeziumIO metadata Debezium source 
{ "connector": "mysql", "version": "3.5.2.Final", "name": "beam-debezium-connector", "database": "inventory", "schema": "mysql-bin.000003", "table": "customers" }
 
{ "version": "3.5.2.Final", "connector": "mysql", "name": "tutorial", "ts_ms": 1791689147000, "snapshot": "false", "db": "inventory", "sequence": null, "ts_us": 1791689147000000, "ts_ns": 1791689147000000000, "table": "customers", "server_id": 223344, "gtid": null, "file": "mysql-bin.000003", "pos": 796, "row": 0, "thread": 13, "query": null }

The missing attributes include pos and row, which we need to remove duplicate data:

  • pos is the position of the change in the MySQL binlog file.

  • row is the row number inside that binlog event, because one event can change many rows.

Together with the file name, they give each change a unique ID. Without pos and row, we can’t reliably find and remove these duplicates in the data warehouse.

DebeziumIO also leaves out ts_ms, which shows when the change was committed in the database. It is very useful for debugging.

Wrapping up

DebeziumIO lets you run change data capture inside an Apache Beam pipeline, without Kafka or Kafka Connect. In this post, we:

  • captured changes from MySQL with DebeziumIO,

  • turned each change into a BigQuery row,

  • wrote the rows to BigQuery, on our own machine and on Dataflow,

  • looked at the metadata that DebeziumIO doesn’t include yet.

DebeziumIO is still experimental, so your feedback really helps.

item.title: Introducing PyDebeziumAI: Real-Time CDC for LangChain and LangGraph
item.dc:creator: Kodukulla Mohnish Mythreya
item.description:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a central pattern in AI application development. The idea is simple: rather than relying solely on an LLM’s pre-trained knowledge, you give it fresh context by retrieving relevant documents from a vector store at query time.

But there is a catch that most tutorials skip over entirely. Where does that vector data come from, and how do you keep it current?

Today, most teams answer that question with a cron job, a nightly batch reload, or a manual re-embedding script. That approach works until the database changes faster than the schedule runs, and your AI starts answering questions based on data that no longer exists or doesn’t reflect a new record committed five minutes ago.

This is the problem that PyDebeziumAI solves. It is an open-source Python library, developed as part of Google Summer of Code 2026 under the Debezium project, that wires Debezium’s Change Data Capture engine directly into LangChain and LangGraph pipelines, ensuring your vector store updates the moment the database does.
item.content:encoded:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a central pattern in AI application development. The idea is simple: rather than relying solely on an LLM’s pre-trained knowledge, you give it fresh context by retrieving relevant documents from a vector store at query time.

But there is a catch that most tutorials skip over entirely. Where does that vector data come from, and how do you keep it current?

Today, most teams answer that question with a cron job, a nightly batch reload, or a manual re-embedding script. That approach works until the database changes faster than the schedule runs, and your AI starts answering questions based on data that no longer exists or doesn’t reflect a new record committed five minutes ago.

This is the problem that PyDebeziumAI solves. It is an open-source Python library, developed as part of Google Summer of Code 2026 under the Debezium project, that wires Debezium’s Change Data Capture engine directly into LangChain and LangGraph pipelines, ensuring your vector store updates the moment the database does.

The infrastructure problem hiding in every RAG pipeline

A conventional, Kafka-based CDC-to-vector pipeline requires managing multiple distributed components (Kafka Connect, Brokers, Schema Registry, and consumers) before a single document reaches your retriever. For a Python developer building an AI application, this complexity is a significant barrier to entry.

PyDebeziumAI takes a different approach by running the Debezium embedded engine directly inside your Python process using pydbzengine (backed by JPype JVM bindings). This eliminates the Kafka broker and Connect overhead entirely, simplifying the architecture significantly.

Every database INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE flows through a Python callback, gets transformed into a LangChain Document, and is upserted or deleted from the vector store, all within the same Python runtime.

Architecture walkthrough

PyDebeziumAI is built in three clean, composable layers.

Ingestion Layer

The ingestion layer bridges the embedded Java engine and Python. ConnectRecordIngestionHandler and JsonIngestionHandler receive raw change records from the Debezium engine callback, convert them into typed Python DebeziumEventModel objects (backed by Pydantic), and route them downstream. This layer also handles all logical type conversions, mapping Debezium’s internal Date, MicroTimestamp, and Decimal types to Python-native float, datetime, and Decimal representations.

Transformation & Mapping Layer

Once a raw change event is a Python object, the transformation layer converts it into a LangChain Document ready for embedding.

  • DocumentBuilder orchestrates the conversion from a DebeziumEventModel to a Document.

  • ProjectionPolicy controls what goes into the document’s page content and metadata using a content template string. For example, Product: $name Category: $category renders as the text embedded in the document.

  • IdStrategy ensures that an update to row id=42 in the database maps to the same document UUID in the vector store every time — making upserts and deletes deterministic and idempotent.

Vector embeddings themselves are generated by an embedding model provider passed directly to the vector store adapter. PyDebeziumAI integrates seamlessly with LangChain’s text embedding ecosystem, supporting cloud-based providers such as OpenAIEmbeddings() as well as local, offline models like HuggingFaceEmbeddings() or sentence-transformers. The adapter passes the formatted page content to the configured embedding provider, producing vector representations that are stored alongside the document metadata.

Synchronization & Compaction Layer

The SyncManager sits at the top of the pipeline. It reads the CDC operation code (c, u, d, r) from each event and calls upsert or delete on the vector store adapter accordingly.

When processing batches under high write load, multiple mutations to the same primary key can arrive in a single flush window. Rather than blindly writing all of them, PyDebeziumAI runs a batch compaction pass before flushing. This collapses redundant sequences:

  • INSERT + UPDATE → single Upsert

  • UPDATE + DELETE → single Delete

  • INSERT + DELETE → skip entirely (the row never needs to reach the vector store)

For embedding generation, the library uses a ThreadPoolExecutor to parallelize calls to the embedding model across documents in a batch.

Quickstart: MySQL to Milvus in under 30 lines

Here is a complete, working example. Given a MySQL inventory.products table, this pipeline will keep a Milvus collection synchronized in real time.

from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings from pydebeziumai.adapters.milvus import MilvusAdapter from pydebeziumai.transformation.document_builder import DocumentBuilder from pydebeziumai.transformation.projection_policy import ProjectionPolicy, TableProjectionPolicy from pydebeziumai.transformation.id_strategy import TablePkIdStrategy from pydebeziumai.sync.manager import SyncManager from pydebeziumai.ingestion.json_handler import JsonIngestionHandler # 1. Define how database rows map to document text and metadata policy = ProjectionPolicy( default=TableProjectionPolicy( content_template="Product: $name
Category: $category
Description: $description", metadata_fields=["id", "category", "price"] ) ) builder = DocumentBuilder( id_strategy=TablePkIdStrategy(pk_fields=["id"]), projection_policy=policy ) # 2. Connect to a Milvus collection (using OpenAI, HuggingFace, or local embeddings) adapter = MilvusAdapter( collection_name="products", embeddings=OpenAIEmbeddings(), # e.g., OpenAIEmbeddings() or HuggingFaceEmbeddings() connection_uri="./local.db" # or a remote Milvus URI ) # 3. Wire up the sync manager and ingestion handler handler = JsonIngestionHandler( sync_manager=SyncManager(vector_store_adapter=adapter, document_builder=builder) ) # 4. Configure and build the embedded engine config = { "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.mysql.MySqlConnector", "database.hostname": "localhost", "database.port": "3306", "database.user": "debezium", "database.password": "dbz", "database.server.id": "184054", "topic.prefix": "dbserver", "table.include.list": "inventory.products" } engine = handler.build_engine(config) engine.run() # Start the replication loop (blocking call)

Any INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on inventory.products will now trigger a corresponding upsert or delete against the Milvus collection, without polling, without Kafka, and without any additional infrastructure.

Pluggable vector store adapters

PyDebeziumAI ships with three production-ready adapters, each supporting bulk operations and metadata filtering:

Adapter Best for

ChromaAdapter

Local development, in-memory prototyping

MilvusAdapter

Large-scale deployments using Milvus Lite or a Milvus server

PGVectorAdapter

Teams already running PostgreSQL who want vector search in the same database

All adapters expose the same interface, so switching between them is a one-line change.

LangGraph integration

PyDebeziumAI exposes retriever wrappers that plug directly into LangChain’s retriever protocol. This means you can use a continuously-synchronized Milvus or Chroma collection as the retriever in any LangChain chain or LangGraph agent, with no adapter shim or custom plumbing needed.

The repository includes two working demonstration agents:

  • RAG chatbot (examples/rag_chatbot/) - a conversational agent answering questions about a live MySQL product catalog.

  • Reactive LangGraph agent (examples/reactive_agent/) - an agent that reacts to incoming CDC events and triggers downstream actions.

Seeing it live: the Streamlit dashboard

To make the zero-lag claim tangible, the library ships with an interactive three-panel Streamlit dashboard (examples/streamlit_dashboard/):

  1. Mutation Console - a form-based UI for inserting, updating, and deleting rows in a MySQL database directly.

  2. WAL Activity Stream - a live-updating feed of raw Debezium change records appearing within milliseconds of each commit.

  3. Semantic Search - a vector search interface querying Milvus in real time, confirming that changes are immediately reflected in retrieval results.

Local benchmarks show the in-process pipeline replicating changes with an end-to-end latency (from database commit to indexed embedding) in the low hundreds of milliseconds.

Getting started

Currently, the library must be installed directly from the GitHub repository until the initial PyPI release is available.

pip install git+https://github.com/debezium/debezium-ai-python.git

To download the required Debezium connector JARs, run the setup tool:

python -m pydebeziumai.tools.setup_jars --connector mysql

Full documentation, including the quickstart guide, API reference, and architecture overview, is available at https://debezium-ai-python.readthedocs.io.

The source code and examples are on GitHub: https://github.com/debezium/debezium-ai-python.

We would love to hear how you are using it — feel free to open an issue, start a discussion, or reach out on the Debezium Zulip chat.

The Google Summer of Code 2026 program has officially concluded for Debezium, and we are delighted to announce that all our contributors successfully passed their final evaluations! 🎉

Over the past few months, our contributors have worked closely with their mentors and the wider community to design, implement, test, and document new capabilities across the Debezium ecosystem.

Their work was not simply an academic exercise or a collection of experimental prototypes. These contributions address real use cases and are already valuable to the many companies and developers who rely on Debezium. The results are included in Debezium 3.7, which was recently released.

Before looking at what comes next, let’s take a moment to celebrate the contributors and the projects they delivered.

The GSoC 2026 projects

This year’s projects explored different areas of the Debezium ecosystem, including developer tooling, deployment, artificial intelligence, vector databases, and new data sources. Each project presented its own technical challenges and created new opportunities for the community.

Debezium CLI

Contributor: Binayak Das
Mentors: Giovanni Panice, Mario Fiore Vitale
Related links: Debezium Design Document

Binayak built a JBang-based CLI (debezium@debezium) to streamline the creation, deployment, and management of CDC pipelines. The build subsystem scaffolds projects, validates configurations, produces trimmed Debezium Server distributions, and creates OCI container images via Jib Core with registry publishing support. The platform subsystem provides multi-environment profile management, connector discovery, live database schema introspection, pipeline signal dispatch, real-time log streaming, and full CRUD operations for connections and transforms.

The Debezium CLI is included in Debezium 3.7 and the documentation available for the next release. Additional commands and integrations planned for future releases.

Host-Based Pipeline Deployment for the Debezium Platform

Contributor: Divyanshu Kumar
Mentors: Mario Fiore Vitale, Giovanni Panice
Related links: Debezium Design Document

Divyanshu extended the Debezium Platform Conductor to deploy CDC pipelines on bare-metal servers, VMs, and cloud instances — not just Kubernetes. He implemented two complementary runtime strategies: Ansible mode, which provisions hosts via playbooks handling SSH discovery and Docker installation, and Agent mode, a lightweight Quarkus HTTP server that runs on each target host and manages Docker containers secured with bearer token authentication. The implementation includes pessimistic host locking, dynamic port allocation, and background polling for container lifecycle management.

The work is included in Debezium 3.7, with potential future support for additional provisioning tools and enhanced monitoring.

PyDebeziumAI

Contributor: Kodukulla Mohnish Mythreya
Mentors: Jiri Pechanec, Vojtěch Juránek
Related links: Debezium Design Document

Mohnish built a Python library that bridges Debezium’s CDC capabilities with the AI ecosystem, enabling sub-second synchronization of vector store embeddings as source data changes. The library ingests events from an embedded Debezium Engine (via pydbzengine), transforms them into LangChain Document objects, and synchronizes them to vector stores (Chroma, PGVector, Milvus) with atomic upserts, soft deletes, and a dead-letter queue. It also includes LangChain-compatible retrievers, LangGraph node integrations, and a Streamlit-based live CDC console.

PyDebeziumAI is included in Debezium 3.7 and published with full documentation on ReadTheDocs.

Debezium Source Connector for Milvus

Contributor: Kartik Angiras
Mentors: Chris Cranford, Giovanni Panice
Related links: Debezium Design Document

Kartik implemented the first CDC source connector for a vector database in the Debezium ecosystem. The connector reads directly from Milvus's internal message queue physical channel (pchannel), requiring Milvus 2.5+ with a Kafka backend. It provides a consistent initial snapshot anchored to an etcd checkpoint and uses a timetick ordering engine for strict TSO-ordered streaming. The connector auto-detects the wire format, maps FloatVector values to a dedicated logical type, supports collection filtering with regex, and exposes JMX metrics.

A complete (Milvus-to-PostgreSQL/pgvector example demonstrates the full pipeline.

The Milvus connector was first released in Debezium 3.7 as incubating, with potential future support for additional MQ backends and update event handling.

Debezium Source Connector for SQLite

Contributor: Siddhant Chaturvedi
Mentors: Vincenzo Santonastaso, Giovanni Panice
Related links: Debezium Design Document

Siddhant implemented an incubating source connector for SQLite using a trigger-based CDC approach. The connector installs AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers on monitored tables, writing change events to an append-only _debezium_cdc_log table — requiring no native extensions, only standard JDBC. It enforces WAL mode for concurrent access, supports multiple snapshot modes, and provides at-least-once delivery with clean resume after restart. Schema change detection via PRAGMA schema_version automatically rebuilds triggers on DDL changes. The connector handles all five SQLite storage classes and includes automatic CDC log compaction.

A complete (SQLite example demonstrates the connector capabilities.

The SQLite connector was first released in Debezium 3.7 as incubating, with potential future support for additional SQLite databases like Turso.

More than a summer project

Although the GSoC program has formally ended, we do not see this milestone as the end of our contributors’ journey with Debezium.

During the program, they became part of the Debezium community. They participated in technical discussions, collaborated with maintainers, received feedback, and contributed capabilities that will be used in real-world environments.

We warmly encourage all our GSoC contributors to remain involved, continue improving their projects, review issues and pull requests, and bring new ideas to the community. Open source contributions do not have to stop when a formal program ends. GSoC introduced the contributors to the project, but the relationships and collaborations built during these months can continue well beyond it.

What’s next

Each contributor prepared a dedicated blog post describing their project. The posts will be published during October, and they should cover the original motivation, the technical approach and the final results.

We also invited the contributors to demonstrate their projects during the Debezium Weekly Forum.

These sessions will give the community an opportunity to:

  • See the new capabilities in action

  • Learn about the technical decisions behind each project

  • Ask questions directly to the contributors

  • Provide feedback based on real-world requirements

  • Explore possible future improvements and contributions

In November 2026, we will conclude this journey with a final showcase bringing together all the GSoC projects.

More details about the presentations and the final showcase will be shared through the official Debezium channels.

Thank you!

Running a successful GSoC program requires much more than writing code. It requires contributors willing to learn and accept feedback, mentors who dedicate their time and experience, and a community that welcomes new participants and supports their growth.

We would like to thank all our contributors for their commitment and hard work throughout the program. We also want to thank the mentors and every community member who reviewed proposals, joined discussions or helped the contributors along the way.

Congratulations again to all our GSoC 2026 contributors for successfully passing their final evaluations!
